frontmatter.title: Introduction
frontmatter.description: Schema Weaver is the first voice-native analytics workspace for PostgreSQL — explore live data, ask Resona AI in plain English, or talk to your database by voice

introduction.content:
Schema Weaver — The First Voice-Native Analytics Workspace for PostgreSQL¶

Connect a database. Browse it in a high-performance grid, ask Resona AI in plain English, or talk to it by voice.

What is Schema Weaver?¶

Two connected surfaces, sharing one account and one set of database connections:

  • Data Explorer — explore live data, and talk to it.
  • SQL Editor — design the schema behind it.

The Two Product Surfaces¶

  • Data Explorer — the analytics workspace. Browse tables, filter and sort live rows, inspect column statistics, ask Resona AI in natural language, talk to your database by voice, build dashboards, and export to CSV, Excel, JSON, SQL, or Google Sheets.

  • SQL Editor
    Write schema, visualize the ER diagram, analyze it with the compiler, and manage migrations against a live database.

Both surfaces share the same database connections, projects, and team memberships. You connect a database once and it is available everywhere.

What You Can Do¶

Data Exploration

  • Browse any table with a high-performance, filterable data grid
  • Filter with typed operators, sort server-side, and hide columns you don't need
  • Analyze columns — null rates, distinct counts, value distributions
  • Ask Resona AI to write queries and build reports from your data
  • Talk to your database — start a voice session and ask questions out loud
  • Generate a dashboard of KPI cards, trends, cohorts, and insights from your whole database
  • Export the current view, selected tables, or an entire schema

Schema Development

  • Write PostgreSQL DDL across multiple files and folders in a structured project
  • See your schema graded and analyzed across 20 quality layers in real time
  • Visualize every table, view, function, and relationship as an interactive ER diagram
  • Use Resona AI to generate SQL, explain schema decisions, and run surgical edits across files

Database Sync

  • Pull the live schema from any PostgreSQL database into your project files
  • Diff your project SQL against the live database before pushing
  • Apply migrations safely — with advisory locking, drift detection, and automatic rollback support
  • Detect when someone changed the database outside of Schema Weaver

Team Collaboration

  • Invite teammates to projects with owner or member roles
  • Share database connections without sharing credentials
  • Track every file edit and migration by author and timestamp

Quick Start¶

  1. Open the Data Explorer and connect a PostgreSQL database
  2. Pick a schema and click a table — your rows load in the grid
  3. Click a column header for statistics, or Filter to narrow rows down
  4. Ask Resona AI a question in plain English, or press the voice orb and ask it out loud
  5. Export the view, a selection of tables, or the whole schema

Already designing a schema? Open the SQL Editor, create a project, add a .sql file, and watch the ER Diagram and Schema Compiler update as you type.

Explore the Documentation¶

  • Data Explorer — live data grid, voice agent, Dashboard AI, Resona AI, exports
  • SQL Editor — files, schema compiler, ER diagram, AI assistant
  • Connector — add connections, pull, diff, push migrations, detect drift
  • Resona AI — models, credits, and how the AI assistant works
  • Team Collaboration — invite members, roles, and shared access

frontmatter.title: Your Connections
frontmatter.description: Manage the PostgreSQL databases your Connector can reach — add them, switch between them, and see which one is currently active

connector/connections.content:
Your Connections¶

Each database your Connector can reach appears as a connection. You switch between them from the selector at the top of the Data Explorer.

Picking a database¶

The selector groups your connections and marks which ones are online. Schema Weaver selects an available one for you when you arrive, and remembers your last choice for next time.

Only online connections are selectable — if the Connector is stopped, its databases won't appear as available.

The dropdown menu gives you:

  • Host provenance: Shows which host connector serves each database (e.g. via vivek-laptop-msi).
  • Live status indicators: Green status badges indicate healthy, online connections.
  • Direct shortcuts: Quickly launch the Connector Dashboard or click + Connect database to attach new instances.

Discovered databases view¶

You can also inspect, search, and manage all databases across your active connectors from the Databases tab in the Connector Dashboard:

From here, you can:

  • Search & Filter: Filter discovered databases by name, alias, or host machine.
  • Inspect Connectivity: Check real-time online status and host connector ID for each database.
  • One-Click Explore: Click Explore → to immediately open any database in the Data Explorer without manually searching through menus.

Adding more databases¶

The Connector can hold more than one. To add another:

pg-connector db add

Run it on the same machine as the existing Connector, then refresh. The new database appears in the selector alongside the others.

To reach something different, run a second Connector on a different machine and register it separately — each one is independent.

Removing a connection¶

Revoking a Connector removes its registration and its databases from Schema Weaver. Your local Connector and its stored credentials are untouched — nothing on your machine changes.

If the Connector is shared with your team, see Sharing with Your Team first, since revoking affects everyone it's shared with.

PostgreSQL only¶

Schema Weaver currently supports PostgreSQL. Other engines aren't supported yet, and there's nothing to configure — the connection type is fixed.

What Schema Weaver stores¶

Just enough to show you the connection and route your queries: a display name, and whether it's currently online. Your host, port, username, password, and certificate never reach Schema Weaver at all.

Security Architecture covers the boundary in full.

Next Steps¶

  • Health & Execution Logs — checking a connection is working
  • Sharing with Your Team — giving colleagues access
  • The Connector — back to the overview

frontmatter.title: Health & Execution Logs
frontmatter.description: Check whether your Connector is online, see its recent activity, and read the queries Schema Weaver has run through it

connector/health.content:
Health & Execution Logs¶

Two panels tell you whether things are working: Health for whether the Connector is reachable, and Execution Logs for what it has actually been asked to do.

Health Monitor¶

The Health tab in the Connector Dashboard monitors latency, daemon connectivity, and query execution health in real time:

Key diagnostic metrics include:

  • Host & Time Scope: Filter metrics by individual connector host or aggregate across all active hosts, scoped over time windows (e.g., Last 1 hour).
  • Relay Status: Outbound WebSocket tunnel state (Active, with active host count).
  • Average Latency: Roundtrip query latency across recent operations with health thresholds (flagging queries above 500ms).
  • P95 Latency: 95th percentile response times to identify tail latency spikes.
  • Success Rate: Percentage of completed queries without database or socket errors.
  • Latency & Response Timeline: Interactive histogram displaying recent query samples with color-coded response buckets:
    • < 100ms (Green): Optimal response time
    • < 500ms (Blue): Normal query execution
    • > 500ms (Orange / Red): Elevated latency

Each Connector also reports an overall state:

StateWhat it means
OnlineRunning, connected to relay, and answering queries
OfflineNot running or unreachable
RevokedRegistration or key was removed

Execution Logs¶

The Execution Logs tab provides a real-time audit trail of every database interaction Schema Weaver performs through your connector:

Key Features:¶

  • Category Filtering: Quickly filter events between All, Queries (data reads and user SQL), Schema (introspections, table catalogs, column stats), and Export.
  • Search: Filter live events by table name, column, or SQL keyword.
  • Execution Telemetry:
    • Operation & Category: Badges distinguish raw QUERY operations from SCHEMA catalog probes.
    • Target Objects: Shows targeted tables (e.g. admin_chat, pg_stats).
    • Result Size: Exact row count returned (e.g. 500 rows, 12 rows).
    • Execution Duration: Millisecond timer badges (e.g. 1949ms, 1116ms).
    • One-Click Copy: Copy the exact SQL statement directly to your clipboard for local testing.

Logs are held in-memory and buffered locally on your connector daemon, so what is recorded is strictly operational telemetry without storing permanent table snapshots in the cloud.

Using them to debug¶

Most connection problems show up here:

What you seeWhat it usually means
No recent entriesNothing has run yet — the Connector may not be receiving work
Failing statementsThe SQL is being rejected; the message says why
Queries but no resultsThe query ran and matched nothing
Nothing at allThe Connector is offline — check Install & Run

What is recorded¶

Operational detail about running queries — statement text, duration, row counts, success or failure, and Connector events. It isn't a copy of your data, and it doesn't contain your credentials.

See Security Architecture for exactly what crosses the boundary and what doesn't.

Next Steps¶

  • Your Connections — switching between databases
  • Install & Run — getting the Connector running
  • The Connector — back to the overview

frontmatter.title: The Connector
frontmatter.description: The Schema Weaver Connector is a small service that runs inside your environment and reaches your PostgreSQL database on your behalf — so your credentials never have to leave it

headings.title: Why it runs on your side

connector.content:
The Connector¶

Schema Weaver reaches your database through the Connector — a small service you run yourself, on the machine that already has access to PostgreSQL.

Everything else in Schema Weaver depends on it. Browse a table, run a query, build a dashboard — all of it goes through the Connector first.

The Connector Dashboard¶

The built-in Connector Dashboard gives you full visibility into your local daemons and database communications:

  • Connectors: Active host connectors (e.g. vivek-laptop-msi) and their online state.
  • Relay Status: Live outbound WebSocket tunnel heartbeat directly connecting your machine to Schema Weaver.
  • Response Latency: Real-time roundtrip query latency tracking execution performance.
  • Query Activity: Total executed statements and current execution success rate.
  • Recent Query Activity: Live snapshot of incoming queries and schema probes with statement duration and timestamps.

Why it runs on your side¶

Your database credentials are the sensitive part, so they never leave your environment. The Connector authenticates locally, and Schema Weaver talks to the Connector instead of to your database.

That's the whole idea: cloud orchestration on one side, your credentials on the other, and nothing in between holding both.

You can read how that boundary is enforced in Security Architecture.

What you put in¶

Exactly two values, both generated by the Connector itself:

ValueWhat it is
Connector IDIdentifies this Connector to Schema Weaver. Starts with agt_
Connection KeyThe secret that authorises it. Starts with swagt_

That's it. Schema Weaver never asks you for a database host, port, username, or password — there is no field for it anywhere in the product. Your database details stay in the Connector's own configuration.

What it does¶

  • Holds your database credentials locally
  • Keeps the connection open and reports whether it's healthy
  • Runs the queries Schema Weaver asks for, and returns results
  • Carries operational telemetry back, so you can see what ran

What you'll need¶

  • Node.js 18 or newer
  • A PostgreSQL database reachable from the machine you run it on
  • About five minutes

Next Steps¶

  • Install & Run — set it up and connect the first database
  • Your Connections — managing what it can reach
  • Security Architecture — how the boundary is enforced

frontmatter.title: Install & Run
frontmatter.description: Install the Schema Weaver Connector CLI on your machine, run it as a 24/7 background service, and register it with Schema Weaver

connector/install.content:
Install & Run¶

Setting up the Connector takes two parts: running it on your host machine or private VPC, then registering it in Schema Weaver.

1 — Installation¶

Open a terminal on the machine that has network access to your PostgreSQL database. You can install the CLI globally or run it directly without installing.

Option A: Global Installation (Recommended)¶

npm i -g @schema-weaver/pg-connector

Option B: Zero-Install (Run via npx)¶

If you prefer not to install global packages or are running in an ephemeral container:

npx @schema-weaver/pg-connector init
npx @schema-weaver/pg-connector db add
npx @schema-weaver/pg-connector start

Node.js 18 or newer is required.

The CLI binary is available under pg-connector (with aliases sw-agent, db-connector, and schemaweaver also included).

2 — Quick Setup Workflow¶

Run these commands on your machine:

pg-connector init                  # generates your Connector ID and Connection Key
pg-connector db add                # attach your PostgreSQL database
pg-connector start                 # launch the connector process
  1. init: Generates a cryptographically secure Connector ID (e.g. agt_...) and Connection Key (e.g. swagt_...). Save these for registration.
  2. db add: Interactively prompts for your local PostgreSQL host, port, database name, and user credentials. All connection parameters and passwords stay local on your machine and are never transmitted to Schema Weaver cloud.
  3. start: Opens a secure, outbound-only WebSocket to the Schema Weaver relay (Port 443).

3 — Register in Schema Weaver¶

In Schema Weaver, click + Add Connector or open the connector menu and follow the guided 3-step registration:

StepWhat you do
1. Setup CLIRun npm i -g @schema-weaver/pg-connector, pg-connector init, and attach your database
2. Register KeyPaste your Connector ID (agt_...) and Connection Key (swagt_...), then click Verify & Connect
3. ConnectedSchema Weaver verifies outbound reachability and displays all discovered databases

Retrieving your credentials: If you already initialized your connector earlier and need your credentials again, run:

pg-connector config --token

This prints your existing Connector ID and token directly from your local config.

The Connection Key is verified over encrypted TLS and never stored in plain text by Schema Weaver.

4 — 24/7 Autostart Services (Persistent Background Daemon)¶

When running on a production server or desktop, you often want the connector to start automatically on system boot and stay alive even if your terminal closes or user logs out.

Native System Service (pg-connector service)¶

pg-connector includes a built-in cross-platform service manager:

# Install and register the background service
pg-connector service install

# Check the live daemon status
pg-connector service status

# Remove the background service
pg-connector service uninstall

Platform implementation details:

  • Linux: Configures and registers a systemd user service (schema-weaver-connector.service) with automatic restart on failure (Restart=always).
  • macOS: Configures a launchd user daemon plist (dev.schemaweaver.pg-connector.plist) with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive.
  • Windows: Configures a persistent Windows Scheduled Task (SchemaWeaverConnector) that triggers on user logon.

PM2 Process Manager¶

If your team already uses PM2 for process supervision, you can easily supervise the connector:

pm2 start pg-connector --name pg-connector -- start
pm2 save
pm2 startup

5 — CLI Diagnostic Debugger¶

If a connection fails or you are setting up in a restrictive corporate network, run the built-in diagnostic tool:

pg-connector debug

The debugger runs an automated 6-point pre-flight checklist:

  • Runtime Check: Node.js engine compatibility (18+) and host OS details.
  • Config Integrity: Validates local configuration file (config.json) and token formats.
  • Relay Reachability: Tests DNS resolution, SSL handshake, and WebSocket handshake to wss://api.schemaweaver.dev (Port 443).
  • PostgreSQL Connectivity: Verifies local network reachability, DNS/IP fallback (IPv4/IPv6), and database authentication for each configured database.
  • Corporate Proxy: Inspects active HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and NO_PROXY environment variables.

6 — Enterprise VPC & Restricted Environments¶

pg-connector is purpose-built for zero-trust private clouds and internal VPCs:

  • Zero Inbound Ports: The connector makes outbound connections only to api.schemaweaver.dev:443. No firewall inbound holes, reverse proxies, or public IP addresses are required.
  • Corporate Proxy Support: Respects system proxy environment variables: 
    export HTTPS_PROXY="http://proxy.internal.corp:8080"
export NO_PROXY="localhost,127.0.0.1,internal.corp"
  • Custom Config Directory: For hardened environments where home directories are restricted: 
    export PG_CONNECTOR_HOME="/opt/schema-weaver/config"
pg-connector start

# Install & Run

Setting up the Connector takes two parts: running it on your host machine or private VPC, then registering it in Schema Weaver.

---

## 1 — Installation

Open a terminal on the machine that has network access to your PostgreSQL database. You can install the CLI globally or run it directly without installing.

### Option A: Global Installation (Recommended)

```bash
npm i -g @schema-weaver/pg-connector
```

### Option B: Zero-Install (Run via npx)

If you prefer not to install global packages or are running in an ephemeral container:

```bash
npx @schema-weaver/pg-connector init
npx @schema-weaver/pg-connector db add
npx @schema-weaver/pg-connector start
```

> **Node.js 18 or newer is required.**
>
> The CLI binary is available under `pg-connector` (with aliases `sw-agent`, `db-connector`, and `schemaweaver` also included).

---

## 2 — Quick Setup Workflow

Run these commands on your machine:

```bash
pg-connector init                  # generates your Connector ID and Connection Key
pg-connector db add                # attach your PostgreSQL database
pg-connector start                 # launch the connector process
```

1. **`init`**: Generates a cryptographically secure **Connector ID** (e.g. `agt_...`) and **Connection Key** (e.g. `swagt_...`). Save these for registration.
2. **`db add`**: Interactively prompts for your local PostgreSQL host, port, database name, and user credentials. All connection parameters and passwords stay local on your machine and are **never** transmitted to Schema Weaver cloud.
3. **`start`**: Opens a secure, outbound-only WebSocket to the Schema Weaver relay (Port 443).

![Connect PostgreSQL Database setup dialog in Schema Weaver showing the terminal setup commands for installing the CLI, initializing keys, adding a database, and starting the daemon](/images/de/connector/add-connector-1.png)

---

## 3 — Register in Schema Weaver

In Schema Weaver, click **+ Add Connector** or open the connector menu and follow the guided 3-step registration:

| Step | What you do |
|---|---|
| **1. Setup CLI** | Run `npm i -g @schema-weaver/pg-connector`, `pg-connector init`, and attach your database |
| **2. Register Key** | Paste your Connector ID (`agt_...`) and Connection Key (`swagt_...`), then click **Verify & Connect** |
| **3. Connected** | Schema Weaver verifies outbound reachability and displays all discovered databases |

![Register Key step in Schema Weaver showing the input fields for Connector ID and Connection Key before verifying and connecting](/images/de/connector/add-connector-2.png)

> **Retrieving your credentials:**
> If you already initialized your connector earlier and need your credentials again, run:
> ```bash
> pg-connector config --token
> ```
> This prints your existing Connector ID and token directly from your local config.

The Connection Key is verified over encrypted TLS and never stored in plain text by Schema Weaver.

---

## 4 — 24/7 Autostart Services (Persistent Background Daemon)

When running on a production server or desktop, you often want the connector to start automatically on system boot and stay alive even if your terminal closes or user logs out.

### Native System Service (`pg-connector service`)

`pg-connector` includes a built-in cross-platform service manager:

```bash
# Install and register the background service
pg-connector service install

# Check the live daemon status
pg-connector service status

# Remove the background service
pg-connector service uninstall
```

Platform implementation details:
- **Linux**: Configures and registers a `systemd` user service (`schema-weaver-connector.service`) with automatic restart on failure (`Restart=always`).
- **macOS**: Configures a `launchd` user daemon plist (`dev.schemaweaver.pg-connector.plist`) with `RunAtLoad` and `KeepAlive`.
- **Windows**: Configures a persistent Windows Scheduled Task (`SchemaWeaverConnector`) that triggers on user logon.

### PM2 Process Manager

If your team already uses **PM2** for process supervision, you can easily supervise the connector:

```bash
pm2 start pg-connector --name pg-connector -- start
pm2 save
pm2 startup
```

---

## 5 — CLI Diagnostic Debugger

If a connection fails or you are setting up in a restrictive corporate network, run the built-in diagnostic tool:

```bash
pg-connector debug
```

The debugger runs an automated 6-point pre-flight checklist:
- **Runtime Check**: Node.js engine compatibility (18+) and host OS details.
- **Config Integrity**: Validates local configuration file (`config.json`) and token formats.
- **Relay Reachability**: Tests DNS resolution, SSL handshake, and WebSocket handshake to `wss://api.schemaweaver.dev` (Port 443).
- **PostgreSQL Connectivity**: Verifies local network reachability, DNS/IP fallback (IPv4/IPv6), and database authentication for each configured database.
- **Corporate Proxy**: Inspects active `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `NO_PROXY` environment variables.

---

## 6 — Enterprise VPC & Restricted Environments

`pg-connector` is purpose-built for zero-trust private clouds and internal VPCs:

- **Zero Inbound Ports**: The connector makes **outbound connections only** to `api.schemaweaver.dev:443`. No firewall inbound holes, reverse proxies, or public IP addresses are required.
- **Corporate Proxy Support**: Respects system proxy environment variables:
  ```bash
  export HTTPS_PROXY="http://proxy.internal.corp:8080"
  export NO_PROXY="localhost,127.0.0.1,internal.corp"
  ```
- **Custom Config Directory**: For hardened environments where home directories are restricted:
  ```bash
  export PG_CONNECTOR_HOME="/opt/schema-weaver/config"
  pg-connector start
  ```

---

## If something looks wrong

| Symptom | Diagnosis & Fix |
|---|---|
| **No connectors listed** | The Connector daemon is not running. Run `pg-connector start` or `pg-connector service install`. |
| **Verification fails** | Confirm the Connector ID starts with `agt_` and the Connection Key starts with `swagt_`. Re-run `pg-connector init` if necessary. |
| **Online but no databases found** | Run `pg-connector db test` locally to test credentials, or `pg-connector db add` to register databases. |
| **Connection times out behind firewall** | Run `pg-connector debug` to verify outbound access to port 443 and inspect `HTTPS_PROXY` settings. |

---

## Next Steps

- [Your Connections](/connector/connections) — managing multiple attached databases
- [Security Architecture](/connector/security-architecture) — zero-ingress security model and credential isolation
- [Health & Execution Logs](/connector/health) — monitoring query execution and daemon health
- [Sharing with Your Team](/connector/sharing) — sharing databases securely with team members

connector/security-architecture.content:
Security Architecture¶

Schema Weaver's database connector is built around two core architectural principles:

  • Local Credential Boundary (LCB): Customer database credentials remain completely isolated inside the customer's private environment.
  • Connector-Enforced Read-Only Execution (CERO): Read-only database access is independently enforced at the connector boundary, never entrusted solely to the cloud or an AI model.

Together, LCB and CERO establish a clear separation between credential ownership, database execution authority, cloud orchestration, and AI-powered analysis.

1. Local Credential Boundary (LCB)¶

Customer-Owned Credential Boundary¶

Under the Local Credential Boundary (LCB), sensitive database credentials stay inside your environment and are never transmitted to Schema Weaver's cloud application layer.

The connector establishes and maintains the PostgreSQL connection locally using credentials controlled exclusively by you.

The following authentication materials never leave your host machine or VPC:

  • Database host and port
  • Database username and password
  • Full connection strings (postgres://...)
  • SSL root certificates, client certificates, and private keys

Schema Weaver Cloud instead identifies and authorizes connections using connector-scoped tokens — a Connector ID (agt_...) and Connection Key (swagt_...) generated locally by the connector itself. These keys identify the connector tunnel; they have zero ability to authenticate to your PostgreSQL database.

Architectural Principle: Credentials stay with the customer.
The cloud control plane never possesses your database credentials. This creates an unbridgeable security boundary between cloud orchestration and database authentication.

2. Connector-Enforced Read-Only Execution (CERO)¶

The Connector as the Execution Security Boundary¶

The connector is not a passive network pipe — it is the database execution boundary.

Every database operation follows this unidirectional security path:

    Schema Weaver Cloud / Resona AI
               │
               │ Controlled query request (TLS 1.3)
               ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │        Schema Weaver Connector         │
   │                                        │
   │  🛡️ Local Credential Boundary (LCB)    │
   │     Credentials remain local           │
   │                                        │
   │  🔒 Read-Only Enforcement (CERO)       │
   │     Local query inspection & checks    │
   └───────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                       │
                       │ Permitted read-only operation only
                       ▼
              Customer PostgreSQL

Under CERO, every incoming SQL request is inspected and evaluated locally by the connector before touching PostgreSQL. For Data Explorer workloads, the connector strictly rejects writes, schema mutations, drops, or unsupported commands at the host boundary.

Database access authority does not originate from what an AI model or cloud application asks for — the local connector remains the final, autonomous enforcement point.

Architectural Principle: Execution stays behind the connector.
An AI model can propose an analytical query, but it receives zero direct authority over the database. The connector validates every query before execution.

3. Separation of Credential Ownership & Execution Authority¶

LCB and CERO create two independent, complementary security boundaries:

  • LCB controls: Who possesses the credentials? → The customer's environment and local connector.
  • CERO controls: What can actually execute? → The connector's local execution policy.
                 SCHEMA WEAVER CLOUD
              ┌───────────────────────┐
              │ Cloud Orchestration   │
              │ AI Analytical Requests│
              │ Telemetry             │
              └───────────┬───────────┘
                          │
                          │ Controlled request (Port 443)
                          ▼
             ┌────────────────────────────┐
             │   Schema Weaver Connector  │
             │                            │
             │ LCB                        │
             │ Credentials remain local   │
             │                            │
             │ CERO                       │
             │ Read-only enforcement      │
             └────────────┬───────────────┘
                          │
                          │ Permitted read-only SQL only
                          ▼
                  CUSTOMER DATABASE

The cloud can request an analytical operation, but it possesses neither your database passwords nor unrestricted database execution authority.

4. Zero-Ingress Network Isolation (Pure Outbound TLS)¶

Traditional database management tools require exposing PostgreSQL to the internet via open inbound firewall ports, public IP addresses, or complex VPN tunnels.

pg-connector eliminates this attack surface entirely using a reverse-polling outbound TLS architecture:

  • 0 Inbound Ports: The connector makes outbound-only connections to api.schemaweaver.dev:443 over TLS 1.3. Your firewall can safely reject 100% of unsolicited inbound traffic.
  • Enterprise Proxy Compatible: Fully respects standard enterprise egress forward proxies (HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, and NO_PROXY).
  • Private VPC & Subnet Deployment: Runs inside private, air-gapped, or NAT-isolated subnets alongside your database without assigning a public IP to either machine.

5. Controlled Data Plane & Transient Query Results¶

The connector creates a controlled, ephemeral data plane between your database and Schema Weaver's cloud services:

CategoryStorage LocationRetention Policy
Database credentialsLocal machine / VPC only (LCB)Never leaves host
Execution policyLocal connector daemon (CERO)Enforced locally on host
Query result rowsTransient communication layerStreamed to active session, never stored as a database replica
Operational telemetrySchema Weaver CloudMetadata only (execution duration, row counts, timestamps, errors)

Query-result rows travel only when needed to render the active view or generate a requested chart/report. Schema Weaver does not maintain a copy or replica of your database.

6. AI-Assisted Analytics Boundary¶

When using Resona AI for analytical questions (identifying trends, generating summaries, comparing records, or building charts), the model receives only the specific result rows required to perform that analysis.

The AI model:

  • Never receives database credentials, hostnames, ports, or connection strings.
  • Never receives unrestricted execution authority over your database.
  • Every query generated by Resona AI is subject to the exact same CERO local policy check before the connector permits it to run.

This boundary is why sharing a connector with team members is completely secure: colleagues can explore and analyze data without anyone having direct access to database passwords. See Sharing with Your Team.

7. Architectural Positioning: The 4 Boundaries¶

Schema Weaver minimizes the trust placed in any individual layer by enforcing four distinct responsibility boundaries:

ResponsibilityBoundaryEnforcement Mechanism
Database credentialsCustomer environmentLocal Credential Boundary (LCB)
Execution authorityLocal connector daemonConnector-Enforced Read-Only (CERO)
Cloud orchestrationSchema Weaver CloudOutbound TLS 1.3 tunnel (api.schemaweaver.dev:443)
Analytical intelligenceConfigured AI modelResona AI scoped analytical context

In Summary¶

  1. Credentials Stay Local (LCB): Passwords and connection strings remain safely inside your infrastructure.
  2. Execution Stays Behind the Connector (CERO): Destructive commands are blocked at the host boundary.
  3. Zero Inbound Ports: Outbound-only TLS over standard port 443 to api.schemaweaver.dev.
  4. Data Moves Only When Required: Query results are transient and never replicated into cloud database storage.

Next Steps¶

  • The Connector — overview of the connector architecture
  • Install & Run — set up the CLI and autostart background daemon
  • Sharing with Your Team — collaborate safely without sharing database credentials
  • Health & Execution Logs — monitoring query execution and audit logs

connector/sharing.content:
Sharing with Your Team¶

A Connector can be shared with your team so colleagues can query the same databases you have. They never see your credentials — they get access to the Connector, which already has them.

What a teammate gets¶

Access to every database that Connector reaches, through the Data Explorer:

  • Browse tables and inspect column statistics
  • Run read-only queries
  • Ask Resona AI questions against your data
  • Build dashboards

They cannot read or write your database credentials, because those never leave your Connector in the first place.

What stays with the owner¶

Whoever registered the Connector keeps administrative control of it. In the Settings tab of the Connector Dashboard, owners can manage credentials and lifecycle options:

Administrative actions available to the owner:

  • Access Level: Displays Owner (You) for the user who registered it. For teammates, management controls are disabled with a note explaining who owns the connector.
  • Registration & Activity: Shows the registration date and the last active timestamp when queries or heartbeats were received.
  • Revoke Credentials: Immediately invalidates the connection secret (swagt_...) to sever tunnel access without deleting connector configurations.
  • Remove Connector: Unregisters the connector daemon and detaches all its databases from Schema Weaver.

If an owner leaves the team or you need to change hands, ownership has to be transferred from their account.

Revoking a shared Connector¶

Revoking or removing a connector detaches it for everyone on the team — that's the behaviour to plan around if others depend on it for exploratory queries or shared dashboards.

Your local Connector installation on your host machine and its stored database passwords remain completely untouched either way.

Managing shared Connectors in Team Settings¶

You can also view, toggle, or unshare connectors directly from the centralized team hub in Settings → Collaboration → Connectors:

This gives team owners and admins a single view of all connector daemons contributing databases to the organization, including their live online heartbeats and agent IDs.

Why not share credentials instead¶

Because there's no need to. A shared Connector gives the same access without anyone handling your database password or connection string. If a teammate leaves, you revoke their access without rotating a credential.

Next Steps¶

  • Team Collaboration — manage members, roles, AI projects, and shared databases
  • Your Connections — what the Connector can reach
  • Security Architecture — the boundary sharing respects
  • The Connector — back to the overview

sql-editor/ai-assistant-tools.content:
AI Tools Reference¶

Resona AI has access to 55 purpose-built tools it can call autonomously when answering your questions. You never call these tools directly — Resona decides which ones to use based on your intent. This page is a complete reference so you know exactly what Resona is capable of.

Quick links: Resona AI Overview · Workspace Editing

How Tools Work¶

When you send a message, Resona's agentic loop plans which tools to call, executes them (up to 10 in parallel per iteration), reads the results, and uses them to form its answer. You see each tool call and its one-line summary in the chat stream.

Safety gates — two tools require your explicit "yes" before executing: db_apply_migration and db_rollback. Resona will always describe the operation and ask for confirmation first.

sql-editor/ai-assistant-workspace.content:
Workspace Editing¶

When Resona AI edits your SQL files it does not regenerate entire files from scratch. It finds the exact block that needs to change and replaces only that — leaving everything else untouched. It can make multiple changes to a single file in one go, or apply edits across several files at once, with full rollback if anything goes wrong.

Quick links: Resona AI Overview · AI Tools Reference · Version History

Three Editing Tools¶

Resona has three editing tools, each suited to a different scope:

ToolScopeWhen Resona uses it
workspace_patch_fileOne change in one fileAdd a column, fix a constraint, insert an index
workspace_apply_diffMultiple changes in one fileAdd several indexes and update a view in the same file
workspace_batch_editChanges across multiple filesRename a column that appears across 4 files

All three support preview mode — Resona can show you a diff before committing anything to your files.

workspace_patch_file — Single Block Edit¶

The most precise tool. Resona finds an exact text block in a file and replaces it. The rest of the file is untouched.

Example: You ask "Add a deleted_at timestamp to the users table."

Resona locates this block in auth.sql:

CREATE TABLE users (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email      text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

And replaces it with:

CREATE TABLE users (
  id         uuid        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email      text        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at timestamptz
);

Only those five lines change. Everything else in auth.sql stays exactly as it was.

After applying, Resona reports the new version number and how many lines changed.

Preview before applying¶

Resona often runs a preview first — showing you the diff in the chat and asking for confirmation before writing. Only after you confirm (or Resona determines the change is safe) does the file update.

workspace_apply_diff — Multiple Changes in One File¶

When several changes need to happen in the same file, this tool applies all of them together. Resona provides an ordered list of find-and-replace pairs.

Example: You ask "Add indexes for all FK columns in billing.sql."

Resona identifies three missing indexes and applies all three to billing.sql in one write:

Change 1: Add index after the orders table definition
Change 2: Add FK index after order_items
Change 3: Add index for invoices.customer_id

All changes are validated before any are written. If one find-and-replace fails to match (e.g. the file was edited since the preview), none of the changes are applied — the file stays clean.

After applying: a single new file version is created containing all three changes.

workspace_batch_edit — Changes Across Multiple Files¶

The broadest editing tool — changes across several files in one call. Each entry in the batch specifies which file to update and what to change (either a full file replacement or a targeted find-and-replace).

Example: You ask "Rename user_id to owner_id across all files."

Resona searches all project files, finds four occurrences, and applies them together:

orders.sql       — column definition
order_items.sql  — view referencing the column
auth.sql         — FK definition in another table
policies.sql     — RLS USING clause

If any change fails, all previous changes in the same batch are rolled back — you never end up with a half-renamed schema.

Mixed operations¶

A batch can combine different operation types:

  • Some files get a targeted find-and-replace (e.g. schema files where one column changes)
  • Other files get a full replacement (e.g. a generated migration file being rebuilt)

If a Change Fails¶

ScenarioWhat happens
workspace_patch_file — text not foundError reported, no changes made
workspace_apply_diff — one pair failsNo changes applied to the file
workspace_batch_edit — one file failsAll successfully-applied changes from that batch are rolled back

In all cases, your files are left in a consistent state — either fully updated or unchanged.

Preview Workflow¶

You can ask Resona to preview before applying anything:

You: Rename full_name to display_name across all files — show me first

Resona: Here are the proposed changes across 3 files:

  auth.sql (1 change):
  - full_name text,
  + display_name text,

  views.sql (2 changes):
  - users.full_name AS author_name
  + users.display_name AS author_name
  ...

  Apply these changes?

You: Yes

Resona: ✓ Applied. New versions created for 2 files.

Version History Integration¶

Every edit creates a new immutable version in Version History. This means:

  • Every AI-applied change is tracked with a timestamp
  • You can always revert to the state before any AI edit
  • The full audit trail is available for any file

If an edit isn't what you wanted, ask Resona to revert:

Revert auth.sql to the version before you renamed the column

Search Before Editing¶

Before any multi-file edit, Resona searches across your project files using workspace_search_files — a regex-capable search. This tells Resona exactly which files are affected before building its edit plan, so it doesn't guess.

Tips¶

  • Be specific about scope: "Add a deleted_at column to @orders only" gives a tighter result than "add soft delete"
  • Ask for preview on risky changes: "Rename this column — show me the diff first"
  • Use version history as your safety net: every pre-edit state is preserved

Next Steps¶

  • Resona AI Overview — the full agentic loop, intent classification, streaming, and memory
  • AI Tools Reference — complete catalog of all 55 tools
  • Version History — browse and restore every version created by AI edits

```sql
  email      text        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at timestamptz
);
```

Only those five lines change. Everything else in `auth.sql` stays exactly as it was.

After applying, Resona reports the new version number and how many lines changed.

### Preview before applying

Resona often runs a preview first — showing you the diff in the chat and asking for confirmation before writing. Only after you confirm (or Resona determines the change is safe) does the file update.

---

## `workspace_apply_diff` — Multiple Changes in One File

When several changes need to happen in the same file, this tool applies all of them together. Resona provides an ordered list of find-and-replace pairs.

**Example:** You ask *"Add indexes for all FK columns in billing.sql."*

Resona identifies three missing indexes and applies all three to `billing.sql` in one write:

```
Change 1: Add index after the orders table definition
Change 2: Add FK index after order_items
Change 3: Add index for invoices.customer_id
```

All changes are **validated before any are written**. If one find-and-replace fails to match (e.g. the file was edited since the preview), none of the changes are applied — the file stays clean.

After applying: a single new file version is created containing all three changes.

---

## `workspace_batch_edit` — Changes Across Multiple Files

The broadest editing tool — changes across several files in one call. Each entry in the batch specifies which file to update and what to change (either a full file replacement or a targeted find-and-replace).

**Example:** You ask *"Rename `user_id` to `owner_id` across all files."*

Resona searches all project files, finds four occurrences, and applies them together:

```
orders.sql       — column definition
order_items.sql  — view referencing the column
auth.sql         — FK definition in another table
policies.sql     — RLS USING clause
```

If any change fails, all previous changes in the same batch are rolled back — you never end up with a half-renamed schema.

### Mixed operations

A batch can combine different operation types:
- Some files get a targeted find-and-replace (e.g. schema files where one column changes)
- Other files get a full replacement (e.g. a generated migration file being rebuilt)

---

## If a Change Fails

| Scenario | What happens |
|---|---|
| `workspace_patch_file` — text not found | Error reported, no changes made |
| `workspace_apply_diff` — one pair fails | No changes applied to the file |
| `workspace_batch_edit` — one file fails | All successfully-applied changes from that batch are rolled back |

In all cases, your files are left in a consistent state — either fully updated or unchanged.

---

## Preview Workflow

You can ask Resona to preview before applying anything:

```
You: Rename full_name to display_name across all files — show me first

Resona: Here are the proposed changes across 3 files:

  auth.sql (1 change):
  - full_name text,
  + display_name text,

  views.sql (2 changes):
  - users.full_name AS author_name
  + users.display_name AS author_name
  ...

  Apply these changes?

You: Yes

Resona: ✓ Applied. New versions created for 2 files.
```

---

## Version History Integration

Every edit creates a new immutable version in [Version History](/sql-editor/version-history). This means:

- Every AI-applied change is tracked with a timestamp
- You can always revert to the state before any AI edit
- The full audit trail is available for any file

If an edit isn't what you wanted, ask Resona to revert:

```
Revert auth.sql to the version before you renamed the column
```

---

## Search Before Editing

Before any multi-file edit, Resona searches across your project files using `workspace_search_files` — a regex-capable search. This tells Resona exactly which files are affected before building its edit plan, so it doesn't guess.

---

## Tips

- **Be specific about scope:** *"Add a deleted_at column to @orders only"* gives a tighter result than *"add soft delete"*
- **Ask for preview on risky changes:** *"Rename this column — show me the diff first"*
- **Use version history as your safety net:** every pre-edit state is preserved

---

## Next Steps

- [Resona AI Overview](/sql-editor/ai-assistant) — the full agentic loop, intent classification, streaming, and memory
- [AI Tools Reference](/sql-editor/ai-assistant-tools) — complete catalog of all 55 tools
- [Version History](/sql-editor/version-history) — browse and restore every version created by AI edits

sql-editor/ai-assistant.content:
Resona AI — SQL Editor¶

Resona AI is an agentic AI assistant built directly into the SQL Editor. It is not a simple chat interface that generates a code block for you to copy — it is a full agentic system with 55 purpose-built tools that can read your files, reason about your schema graph, run the compiler, analyze security and performance, write surgical multi-file edits, diff your live database, and apply migrations — all from a single conversation.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · Tools Reference · Workspace Editing

Opening Resona AI¶

Resona AI is available in two places:

Left Sidebar Panel¶

Click Resona AI in the left sidebar of the SQL Editor to open the full-height chat panel. This is the primary AI interface — it stays open as you navigate files and shows the full conversation history.

ER Diagram Nodes¶

Resona AI is also embedded directly in the ER Diagram as floating chat nodes anchored to individual tables, schema groups, or the full canvas. See Resona AI in the ER Diagram for details.

How It Works — Agentic Loop¶

Unlike a simple prompt → response system, Resona AI uses a ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) agentic loop:

Your message
     ↓
Intent classification
(write SQL / debug / analyze / file action / migrate / …)
     ↓
Context assembly
(schema graph + compiler result + @ mentions + history)
     ↓
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  THINK: Stream LLM response                     │
  │      ↓                                          │
  │  DETECT tool calls in response                  │
  │      ↓                                          │
  │  EXECUTE tools (up to 10 in parallel)           │
  │      ↓                                          │
  │  OBSERVE results → feed back to LLM             │
  │      ↓                                          │
  │  LOOP (up to 10 iterations)                     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     ↓
Validate final SQL (if generated)
     ↓
Stream final answer + usage stats

You see this loop play out in real time: as Resona works, each tool call is shown with its name and a one-line result summary. You can follow along as it reads files, runs the compiler, checks indexes, and builds its answer — step by step.

Intent Classification¶

Before executing any tools, Resona classifies your message into one of ten intent categories:

IntentWhat triggers itTools made available
write_query"Create a table…", "Add a column…"Schema tools, file tools, compiler
debug_query"Why is this FK failing?", "Fix this syntax"Compiler, dependency tools, debug tools
optimize_query"Improve performance", "Missing indexes?"Performance audit, graph tools, compiler
explain_query"What does this trigger do?", "Explain…"Schema tools, compiler, graph tools
refactor_query"Rename this column across files", "Clean up…"Workspace tools, batch edit, compiler
schema_question"How are users and orders connected?"Graph tools, dependency tools
plan_query"How should I model a…", "What's the best approach…"Compiler, graph tools, analysis tools
workspace_action"Create a file", "Show me the file tree"Workspace file tools
database_action"Pull live schema", "Apply migration", "Diff"Migration tools, terminal
conversationalGeneral questions, small talkMinimal toolset

Each intent activates a curated subset of tools — Resona doesn't get all 55 tools for every message, only the ones relevant to what you asked. This keeps responses focused and fast.

Context Awareness¶

Resona automatically receives rich context before every response:

ContextWhat it includes
Full schema graphEvery table, view, function, relationship — from the ER Diagram's compiled output
Compiler resultThe 20-layer compilation: grades, every issue with severity and suggested fix
Project file treeAll files and folders in the active project
Conversation historyCompressed and summarized history across sessions
@ mentionsSpecific tables, files, or folders you reference explicitly
Active fileThe currently open file and cursor context

You do not need to paste your schema into the prompt. Resona already knows it.

@ Mentions¶

Type @ to reference a specific table, file, or folder by name. An autocomplete dropdown filters your project's objects as you type:

What indexes are missing on @orders?
Add a foreign key on @order_items.product_id referencing @products.id
Read @migrations/001_init.sql and explain the changes

What Resona Can Do¶

Schema Generation¶

TaskExample prompt
Create a table"Create a users table with email, hashed password, and created/updated timestamps"
Add columns"Add soft delete support to @orders with deleted_at and deleted_by"
Create an enum"Create an enum for payment methods: card, bank_transfer, crypto, invoice"
Generate RLS"Write RLS policies so users can only see their own rows in @documents"
Create functions"Write a trigger function that updates updated_at on every row change"
Write migrations"Write a migration to rename full_name to display_name across @users and @profiles"
Multi-table design"Design a RBAC system with roles, permissions, and a junction table"

Schema Analysis¶

TaskExample prompt
Security audit"Run a security audit on my schema — show RLS coverage and privilege risks"
Performance audit"Find missing indexes and table bloat estimates"
Normalization check"Is my schema in 3NF? Flag any denormalization"
Naming audit"Check naming consistency across all tables and columns"
Dependency analysis"What breaks if I drop the @products.category_id column?"
Cascade impact"Show the cascade chain from @orders — what gets deleted when an order is deleted?"
Centrality analysis"Which tables are the most critical hubs in the schema?"

Database Operations¶

TaskExample prompt
Pull live schema"Pull the current schema from the connected database"
Diff"Show me the diff between my project SQL and the live database"
Preview migration"Preview what SQL would be applied if I push now"
Apply migration"Apply the pending changes to the database"
Rollback"Roll back the last migration"
Migration history"Show me the last 10 migrations"

Safety gates: Apply migration and Rollback require your explicit confirmation before executing. Resona will always describe what it is about to do and ask "confirm?" before touching your live database.

File Operations¶

TaskExample prompt
Read a file"Read @auth.sql and summarize what's in it"
Create a file"Create a new file called triggers.sql with the audit trigger we just discussed"
Edit a file (surgical)"Add the missing index to @orders.sql — just the index, nothing else"
Multi-file edit"Rename user_id to owner_id in @orders.sql, @order_items.sql, and @views.sql"
Revert a file"Revert @billing.sql to the version from two saves ago"
Search across files"Find all tables that reference the users table across all files"

Streaming — Watch It Think¶

Resona streams its reasoning in real time. As it works through your request, you see:

  • Tool calls: the name of each tool being executed and a one-line result summary
  • Thinking: the LLM's reasoning between tool calls
  • Final answer: the response streamed word by word

This transparency means you always know what Resona is doing — you can see it read a file, run the compiler, check a dependency, and then form its answer. If it takes an unexpected path, you can interrupt and redirect.

Memory — Remembers Across Sessions¶

Resona maintains a persistent memory of your schema conversations. This is a four-layer compression model:

LayerWhat it storesWhen it's used
Recent messagesLast 20 messages verbatimAlways in context
Schema changesDDL operations and migrations appliedRecent history
Conversation summariesLLM-generated summaries of older message clustersOlder sessions
Global factsKey facts extracted from the full conversation historyLong-term memory

When your conversation history grows long, Resona automatically compresses older messages into summaries — so it never loses the thread of what you've been working on, even across sessions or days. The next time you open the SQL Editor, Resona remembers what you were building.

Applying AI-Generated SQL¶

When Resona generates SQL, you have three options:

ButtonAction
Apply to fileInserts (or replaces) the generated SQL into the currently active file
Apply to new fileCreates a new file in the project and writes the SQL there
CopyCopies the SQL to clipboard

Preview Before Applying¶

Before any change is written to a file, a diff overlay shows exactly what will be added or removed — green lines are additions, red are removals. Click Accept to apply or Reject to discard.

Resona can also make surgical edits that target only the specific section of a file that needs changing, rather than replacing the whole file. See Workspace Editing for how this works.

Iterative Refinement¶

Resona maintains full conversation context across turns. You can refine your schema iteratively:

You:   Create a products table with name, price, and stock_qty

AI:    [generates CREATE TABLE products ...]

You:   Add a category_id FK referencing @categories

AI:    [adds column + FK constraint, updates the table]

You:   Now add a partial index for products where stock_qty = 0

AI:    [adds CREATE INDEX ... WHERE stock_qty = 0]

You:   Run the compiler and tell me what issues are left

AI:    [calls sql_compile_schema tool, reports 2 warnings]

You:   Fix both warnings

AI:    [patches the file to resolve both issues]

Each step builds on the last. Resona keeps the full schema state and conversation in context throughout.

Model Selection¶

Click the model selector in the AI panel header:

ModelBest for
Claude SonnetDefault — fast, accurate schema generation, most tasks
Claude OpusComplex multi-table design, deep analysis, very large schemas

Usage and Credits¶

Each AI response consumes credits from your Schema Weaver plan. The footer of the AI panel shows current session usage.

PlanDaily AI credits
Free50
Pro500
Team2,000 per seat

Credits reset at midnight UTC.

Keyboard Shortcuts¶

ShortcutAction
Ctrl+K / Cmd+KOpen AI panel (with selected SQL as context if text is highlighted)
EnterSend message
Shift+EnterNew line in the input
↑Navigate to previous message in input history
EscapeClose the AI panel

Next Steps¶

  • AI Tools Reference — complete catalog of all 55 AI tools with parameters and capabilities
  • Workspace Editing — surgical file edits, multi-file diffs, atomic batch operations
  • Resona AI in the ER Diagram — AI anchored to specific table nodes and schema groups
  • Schema Compiler — the 20-layer analysis engine Resona uses to assess your schema
  • Connector — connect a live database so Resona can pull, diff, and migrate

sql-editor/er-diagram-ai.content:
Resona AI in the ER Diagram¶

Resona AI is embedded directly into the ER Diagram at three levels: individual tables, schema groups, and the full schema. Each level opens a chat panel anchored by a dashed blue edge to its subject — you can ask questions, request SQL, and apply generated changes without leaving the diagram.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · ER Diagram Overview · Resona AI Assistant

Three AI Entry Points¶

ModeHow to openWhat it knows
Table AIClick the ✦ Sparkles icon on any table nodeThe selected table: columns, types, constraints, indexes, triggers, policies
Group AIClick the ✦ AI icon on a schema group header (when grouping is enabled)All tables, views, and objects in that schema group
Global AIClick Resona AI in the toolbarThe entire merged schema — all tables, views, functions, relationships across all files

Each mode opens a separate floating chat node on the canvas, connected to its subject via a dashed blue edge. You can have multiple AI nodes open simultaneously (one per table, one per group, and one global) and move them freely around the canvas.

Table AI¶

Table AI opens a chat panel anchored to a specific table. The AI has full context of:

  • All columns, types, defaults, and nullability
  • Primary key and foreign key definitions
  • All indexes on the table
  • All triggers (timing, events, function)
  • All RLS policies (command, roles, USING, WITH CHECK)
  • All check constraints
  • Inbound and outbound FK relationships (which tables reference this one, and which tables this one references)

Opening Table AI¶

Option A — From the table node:

  1. Hover over any table node
  2. Click the ✦ (Sparkles) icon that appears in the node header
  3. The AI chat panel spawns to the right of the table node, connected with a dashed blue line

Option B — Keyboard shortcut:

  1. Select a table node (click it)
  2. Press Ctrl+K / Cmd+K
  3. Table AI opens for the selected table

Suggested Prompts for Table AI¶

When Table AI opens, it shows quick-start prompts:

  • "Analyze structure" — reviews the table for common design issues (missing PKs, unbounded text columns, nullable FKs without indexes, etc.)
  • "Suggest indexes" — recommends indexes based on the FK columns, common query patterns, and current index coverage
  • "Check normalization" — evaluates whether the table is in 3NF, flags denormalization, and suggests improvements
  • "Generate seed data" — generates realistic INSERT statements for development/testing
  • "Write a migration" — generates the ALTER TABLE DDL to implement a described change safely

Closing Table AI¶

Click the × button on the AI chat node, or click the ✦ Sparkles icon on the same table again to toggle it off.

Group AI¶

Group AI opens when schema grouping is enabled and you click the AI icon on a group container header. The AI has context of every object inside that schema group — tables, views, functions, and their relationships.

Group AI is useful for:

  • Schema-level review — "Are there any design issues across the billing schema?"
  • Cross-table analysis — "How do orders, order_items, and products relate? Is this normalized correctly?"
  • Domain documentation — "Write a markdown summary of what the auth schema contains and how it works"
  • Refactoring suggestions — "Which tables in this schema are candidates for partitioning?"

Global AI¶

Global AI opens by clicking Resona AI in the toolbar. It is anchored in the top-left of the canvas and has context of the entire merged schema — every table, view, function, relationship, and constraint across all files in the project.

Global AI is best for:

  • Full-schema review — "What are the most critical issues in this schema?"
  • Cross-domain questions — "How does the auth schema connect to the billing schema?"
  • Schema generation — "Add a notifications table that can target both users and organizations"
  • Documentation — "Generate a README explaining this database schema"
  • Migration planning — "Plan a safe migration to add multi-tenancy to this schema"

Applying AI-Generated SQL¶

When Resona suggests SQL changes (new tables, ALTER TABLE, new indexes, etc.), you can review and apply them directly from the chat panel:

  1. The AI generates a SQL block with a Preview button
  2. Click Preview to see a diff of how the change would affect your current SQL files
  3. Click Apply to insert the generated SQL into your active file
  4. The ER Diagram updates immediately — new nodes and edges appear as soon as the SQL is parsed

AI-generated SQL is appended to your current file with a -- AI Generated: comment marker so you can find and review it easily.

AI Chat Context¶

Each AI node maintains its own conversation history. You can:

  • Continue the conversation — ask follow-up questions that build on the previous exchange
  • Start a new chat — click New Chat in the panel to reset the conversation while keeping the panel open
  • View history — scroll up in the panel to see earlier messages in the session

The AI automatically receives the latest version of your schema each time you send a message — if you edit SQL between messages, the AI sees the updated schema.

Working with Multiple AI Nodes¶

You can have multiple AI nodes open simultaneously:

  • One Global AI node
  • One AI node per table (open as many tables as you want)
  • One AI node per schema group

Each node is independent — conversations don't cross-contaminate. This lets you, for example, ask Global AI about the overall architecture while simultaneously asking Table AI on orders about a specific index strategy.

Move any AI node by dragging it. Nodes stay connected to their subject via the dashed blue edge regardless of where you drag them.

ShortcutAction
Ctrl+K / Cmd+KOpen Table AI for the currently selected table node
EscapeClose the most recently opened AI node

sql-editor/er-diagram-grouping.content:
Grouping & Schema Clusters¶

When Cluster by Schema is enabled, the ER Diagram groups all nodes by their PostgreSQL schema namespace into visually distinct containers. Tables, views, functions, and other objects that belong to auth, billing, public, inventory — or any other schema in your project — are enclosed in their own labeled group. This makes it immediately clear which domain each object belongs to and eliminates the visual noise of a flat diagram with hundreds of nodes.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · ER Diagram Overview

Enabling Grouping¶

  1. In the diagram footer, click the Group button
  2. Select Cluster by Schema
  3. The diagram re-runs ELK layout in two-level hierarchical mode — groups are positioned first, then their contents are laid out inside each group

To disable grouping, click Group → Cluster by Schema again. The diagram returns to a flat layout.

Group Containers¶

Each schema group is rendered as a resizable container with a colored header:

Header¶

ElementDescription
Schema nameThe PostgreSQL schema name (e.g. auth, billing, public)
Color barEach schema gets a consistent color derived from its name — the same color is used everywhere that schema appears in the UI
Tables badgeCount of table nodes inside the group
Views badgeCount of view/materialized view nodes inside the group
Relations badgeCount of foreign-key edges whose both endpoints are inside the group

Resizing Groups¶

Drag the resize handle at the corner or edge of a group container to make it larger or smaller. This is useful when a group has many tables and the auto-layout makes it too compact to read comfortably.

Click Auto-fit (available via right-click on the group header) to automatically resize the container to snugly fit all its children.

Moving Groups¶

Drag the group header to reposition the entire group — all nodes inside it move together. When groups are repositioned, the cross-group FK edges update automatically to connect through the new positions.

Locking Groups¶

Once you've arranged your group containers in a useful layout, enable Lock Groups to prevent accidental repositioning:

  1. Click Group in the footer
  2. Select Lock Groups

With groups locked:

  • Group containers cannot be dragged
  • Individual nodes inside a group can still be dragged within their container
  • Re-running auto-layout will reposition nodes inside groups but respect group positions

Cross-Schema Relationships¶

Foreign keys that cross schema boundaries (e.g. billing.orders.user_id → auth.users.id) are drawn as edges that exit one group container and enter another. These cross-group edges are particularly useful for understanding which schemas are tightly coupled.

The edge passes through the group borders with routing that avoids overlapping node labels.

Schema Color Coding¶

Each schema gets a persistent color that is used consistently:

  • In the group container header background
  • On the schema badge shown on table node headers when a table's schema is not public
  • In the Visibility panel schema group list

The color is derived deterministically from the schema name, so auth always gets the same color regardless of project.

Two-Level ELK Layout¶

When grouping is enabled, the ELK layout engine runs a two-level hierarchical algorithm:

  1. Intra-group layout: nodes within each schema are laid out relative to each other, respecting FK directions
  2. Inter-group layout: groups are positioned on the canvas to minimize cross-group edge crossings

This two-level approach means that within-schema FK chains are readable (parent tables above child tables), while across-schema dependencies flow in the overall chosen direction (LR, TB, etc.).

Note: Two-level hierarchical layout has an 8-second timeout. For very large schemas (hundreds of tables across many schemas), the layout may fall back to a flat arrangement. Use Visibility Controls to hide non-essential object types and reduce node count.

Tips for Working with Groups¶

  • Name your schemas intentionally — the group header shows the raw PostgreSQL schema name, so billing, auth, inventory produce cleaner diagrams than schema1, schema2
  • Use locking after initial layout — run auto-layout once, fine-tune group positions, then lock to prevent accidents
  • Use the Visibility panel to declutter — if a schema group has many auxiliary objects (sequences, policies, roles), hide those node types to reduce group density
  • Cross-group edges reveal coupling — a schema group with many cross-group edges is tightly coupled to other schemas, which is useful to know before refactoring
  • Resize before exporting — auto-fit each group before exporting as PNG/SVG to ensure nothing is clipped

Next Steps¶

  • ER Diagram Overview — full feature overview including navigation, layout, and export
  • Visibility & Node Types — control which schemas and object types are shown inside groups
  • Resona AI in the ER Diagram — open AI chat anchored to a specific schema group for domain-level analysis
  • Path Analysis — trace the shortest FK path across schema boundaries

sql-editor/er-diagram-path-analysis.content:
Path Analysis¶

Path Analysis finds the shortest foreign-key relationship chain between any two tables in your schema. Instead of manually tracing JOIN paths through a dense diagram, you select a start table and an end table — the diagram highlights every intermediate table and edge you would need to traverse to connect them.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · ER Diagram Overview

When to Use Path Analysis¶

  • Writing multi-table JOINs — when you know the start and end tables but need to figure out which intermediate tables to join through
  • Understanding a legacy schema — quickly visualize how two distant parts of a schema are connected
  • Reviewing migrations — check whether a new table is connected to the rest of the graph as expected
  • Onboarding — help new team members understand how the data model hangs together

Activating Path Analysis¶

  1. Click the Path button in the diagram toolbar (footprints icon)
    • The toolbar button turns highlighted to indicate path mode is active
    • A draggable Path Analysis overlay appears on the canvas
  2. Click any table node to set it as the start table
  3. Click a second table node to set it as the end table
  4. The path is calculated and highlighted immediately

Reading the Result¶

When a path is found, the diagram:

  • Highlights every node in the path with a distinct color
  • Highlights every edge in the path
  • Dims all nodes and edges that are not part of the path
  • Shows the full step-by-step path in the overlay panel

Each step in the overlay shows:

FieldDescription
SourceThe table at the start of this hop
TargetThe table at the end of this hop
RelationshipThe foreign key or relationship connecting them
DirectionWhether the FK points from source → target or target → source

Path Algorithms¶

The overlay lets you choose between two algorithms:

BFS — Breadth-First Search¶

Best for most cases. BFS finds the path with the fewest hops — it treats all FK relationships as equal regardless of confidence, and returns the shortest chain by number of intermediate tables.

Use BFS when:

  • You want the simplest possible JOIN path
  • All relationships in your schema are explicit FKs (not inferred)
  • You need a fast result on a large schema

Dijkstra — Weighted Shortest Path¶

Best for inferred or mixed-confidence schemas. Dijkstra treats each relationship edge as having a weight based on confidence. Higher-confidence relationships (explicit FKs) are preferred over lower-confidence inferred relationships.

Use Dijkstra when:

  • Your schema contains inferred relationships (e.g. matching column names without explicit FKs)
  • You want the most reliable path, not just the shortest by hop count
  • You're working with a schema that was imported or reverse-engineered

Filter Options¶

Click the settings gear icon in the Path Analysis overlay to open filter controls:

FilterDescription
Exclude inferred relationshipsSkips edges of type VIEW_DEPENDENCY, TRIGGER_TARGET, and INFERRED — only uses explicit FK edges
Exclude low-confidence edgesSkips any relationship with confidence below 0.8

These filters affect both the path calculation and the diagram highlighting. Using both filters together gives you a path built entirely from explicit, high-confidence FK relationships.

Path Cost¶

When using the Dijkstra algorithm, the overlay shows a path cost — the cumulative weight of all edges in the path. Lower cost means higher overall confidence. This is useful for comparing alternative paths between the same two tables.

No Path Found¶

If no FK chain connects the two selected tables, the overlay shows "No path found." This can mean:

  • The tables are in completely separate parts of the schema (no FK chain at all)
  • The path exists only through inferred/low-confidence relationships, and those are currently filtered out — try disabling the filters
  • One or both tables are views or non-table objects that don't participate in FK relationships

Resetting Path Analysis¶

ActionHow
Clear selectionClick Reset in the overlay, or click the same table again
Exit path modeClick the Path button in the toolbar again — the overlay closes and the diagram returns to normal
Change start or endClick a different table while in path mode — the selection updates automatically

Next Steps¶

  • ER Diagram Overview — full feature overview including navigation, layout, and export
  • Grouping & Schema Clusters — cluster your schema by PostgreSQL namespace
  • Resona AI in the ER Diagram — ask AI to explain the join path or generate the JOIN SQL
  • Visibility & Node Types — hide irrelevant object types before running path analysis on a large schema

| **Exclude inferred relationships** | Skips edges of type VIEW_DEPENDENCY, TRIGGER_TARGET, and INFERRED — only uses explicit FK edges |
| **Exclude low-confidence edges** | Skips any relationship with confidence below 0.8 |

These filters affect both the path calculation and the diagram highlighting. Using both filters together gives you a path built entirely from explicit, high-confidence FK relationships.

---

## Path Cost

When using the Dijkstra algorithm, the overlay shows a **path cost** — the cumulative weight of all edges in the path. Lower cost means higher overall confidence. This is useful for comparing alternative paths between the same two tables.

---

## No Path Found

If no FK chain connects the two selected tables, the overlay shows "No path found." This can mean:

- The tables are in completely separate parts of the schema (no FK chain at all)
- The path exists only through inferred/low-confidence relationships, and those are currently filtered out — try disabling the filters
- One or both tables are views or non-table objects that don't participate in FK relationships

---

## Resetting Path Analysis

| Action | How |
|---|---|
| **Clear selection** | Click **Reset** in the overlay, or click the same table again |
| **Exit path mode** | Click the **Path** button in the toolbar again — the overlay closes and the diagram returns to normal |
| **Change start or end** | Click a different table while in path mode — the selection updates automatically |

---

## Next Steps

- [ER Diagram Overview](/sql-editor/er-diagram) — full feature overview including navigation, layout, and export
- [Grouping & Schema Clusters](/sql-editor/er-diagram-grouping) — cluster your schema by PostgreSQL namespace
- [Resona AI in the ER Diagram](/sql-editor/er-diagram-ai) — ask AI to explain the join path or generate the JOIN SQL
- [Visibility & Node Types](/sql-editor/er-diagram-visibility) — hide irrelevant object types before running path analysis on a large schema
