sql-editor/er-diagram-visibility.content:
Visibility & Node Types¶

The ER Diagram supports every PostgreSQL object type — tables, views, materialized views, functions, enums, domains, roles, sequences, extensions, and RLS policies. On a real production schema this can mean dozens or hundreds of extra nodes beyond your core tables. The Visibility controls let you show only what you need, making large diagrams readable and layout faster.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · ER Diagram Overview

Opening Visibility Controls¶

Click Visibility in the diagram footer (bottom-right area). A dropdown opens with two sections: Node Types and Schema Groups.

Changes apply immediately — nodes that are toggled off disappear from the canvas and the layout reflows. Toggle them back on to restore them.

Node Types¶

The Node Types section lets you show or hide each category of PostgreSQL object:

Node TypeDefaultWhat is hidden when off
Views✅ OnRegular CREATE VIEW nodes and the edges representing view dependencies
Materialized Views✅ OnCREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW nodes
Functions✅ OnCREATE FUNCTION and CREATE PROCEDURE nodes
Enums✅ OnCREATE TYPE … AS ENUM nodes
Domains✅ OnCREATE DOMAIN nodes
Roles✅ OnCREATE ROLE nodes
Sequences✅ OnCREATE SEQUENCE nodes
Extensions✅ OnCREATE EXTENSION nodes
Policies✅ OnCREATE POLICY (RLS policy) nodes

All types are on by default. For most schema review workflows, you'll want to keep Views and Enums on (they often have FK-like relationships with tables) and consider turning off Roles, Sequences, Extensions, and Policies to reduce clutter.

Recommended Visibility Profiles¶

For a clean table-focused view:

  • Turn off: Functions, Roles, Sequences, Extensions, Policies
  • Keep on: Views, Materialized Views, Enums, Domains

For security review:

  • Turn off: Functions, Sequences, Extensions
  • Keep on: Tables, Views, Policies, Roles

For maximum density (large schemas):

  • Turn off: Functions, Roles, Sequences, Extensions, Policies, Domains
  • Use TITLE view mode on table nodes
  • Use schema grouping to cluster by namespace

For migration review:

  • Keep everything on
  • Use Focus mode on the changed table instead of hiding types

Schema Groups¶

The Schema Groups section lists every PostgreSQL schema namespace present in your project. Each schema has its own toggle:

StateEffect
✅ CheckedAll objects in that schema are visible
☐ UncheckedAll objects in that schema are hidden — tables, views, functions, enums, everything

Common Use Cases¶

Hide system schemas: If your schema includes pg_catalog or information_schema objects, hide them here to keep the diagram focused on your application schema.

Focus on one domain: In a multi-schema project with auth, billing, inventory, and public, you can hide auth and inventory to focus the diagram on billing only.

Temporary hide during layout: Hiding a large schema temporarily can speed up ELK layout if you're working on a different part of the diagram.

Active Filter Badge¶

When any schema is hidden, an amber badge appears in the diagram footer showing how many schemas are currently filtered:

● 2 schemas hidden    ×

Click the × on this badge to instantly unhide all schemas and restore the full diagram.

Column View Mode¶

In addition to showing/hiding entire node types, you can control how much detail is shown inside each table node. Switch between view modes using the selector in the diagram footer:

ModeWhat columns showBest for
ALLEvery column with name, type, constraints, collapsible index/trigger/policy sectionsDetailed review, documentation
KEYSOnly primary key and foreign key columnsUnderstanding relationships at a glance
TITLETable name only — no columns shownVery large schemas, high-level overviews

View mode applies globally to all table, view, and materialized view nodes at once.

Visibility and Layout¶

Every time you toggle a node type or schema, the visible node count changes and ELK re-runs layout for the remaining nodes. This means:

  • Turning things off makes the diagram denser around the remaining nodes — run Fit to recenter
  • Turning things back on re-adds nodes; their positions are computed from scratch for the new layout unless you have manually dragged them

Tip: Set your visibility profile first, then run auto-layout (Layout → Re-run auto-layout) once to get a clean arrangement. After that, manually drag any nodes you want to reposition and lock groups if you're using schema grouping.

Visibility and Path Analysis¶

Path Analysis respects the current visibility settings. If a schema or node type is hidden, tables in that hidden set are excluded from path calculation. This means:

  • Hiding a schema will make paths that pass through that schema return "No path found"
  • Hiding object types like Views removes view dependency edges from path calculation
  • Use Exclude inferred relationships in the path analysis settings instead of hiding schemas if you want to keep all tables visible but ignore certain edge types

Next Steps¶

  • ER Diagram Overview — full feature overview including navigation, export, and all node type details
  • Grouping & Schema Clusters — cluster visible nodes by schema namespace
  • Path Analysis — find shortest join paths through visible tables
  • Resona AI in the ER Diagram — AI analysis scoped to visible tables and schemas

sql-editor/er-diagram.content:
ER Diagram¶

The ER Diagram is a live, interactive visualization of your entire PostgreSQL schema. Every object — tables, views, materialized views, functions, enums, domains, sequences, roles, extensions, and RLS policies — renders as a node on a pannable, zoomable canvas. Foreign-key relationships appear as directed edges. The diagram updates in real time as you type SQL with no manual refresh required, and scales to schemas with thousands of tables.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · Path Analysis · Grouping · AI Features

Opening the Diagram¶

The ER Diagram is built into the SQL Editor — there is no separate page to navigate to.

  • In standard mode: Click Graph in the footer status bar — the diagram opens as a full-screen overlay
  • In fullscreen / split mode: The diagram opens as a resizable panel alongside the editor, updating as you type
  • Keyboard shortcut: Ctrl+G / Cmd+G toggles the diagram panel

How the Diagram is Built¶

The diagram is generated entirely in the browser from the same compiled schema that feeds the Schema Compiler. No server round-trip is needed.

All project SQL files
        ↓
  Schema Weaver Custom SQL Parser
  (runs entirely in your browser — no server round-trip)
        ↓
  Schema Compiler (20 layers)
        ↓
  Relationship Graph
  (foreign keys, view deps, trigger targets, inferred)
        ↓
  ELK Auto-Layout Engine
        ↓
  React Flow Canvas
  (re-renders on every SQL change)

Custom parser: Schema Weaver uses its own purpose-built PostgreSQL SQL parser that runs entirely in the browser. This is not a thin wrapper around a generic parser — it is a custom multi-phase parser designed specifically for DDL (schema definitions), handling PostgreSQL-specific syntax for partitions, RLS, identity columns, generated columns, domain types, and more. Because everything runs client-side, there is zero latency between typing SQL and seeing the diagram update.

Because the pipeline is entirely client-side, the diagram is always in sync with your code — add a CREATE TABLE, a new node appears immediately; add a REFERENCES clause, a new edge appears immediately.

Supported PostgreSQL Objects¶

The ER Diagram renders every major PostgreSQL object type as a distinct node:

Node TypeVisualWhat it shows
TableWhite/gray cardAll columns with types, constraints, PKs, FKs, indexes, triggers, policies, check constraints
ViewDashed border cardColumn count, source query context, Eye icon
Materialized ViewDashed border with refresh iconColumn count, REFRESH CONCURRENTLY command tooltip
Function / ProcedureCode cardReturn type, PROC/FUNC badge, argument types
EnumType cardAll enum values displayed as colored badges
DomainType cardBase type, NOT NULL constraint, CHECK expression
SequenceSequence cardStart value, increment, min/max bounds
RoleRole cardAttributes as badges: SUPERUSER, LOGIN, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, BYPASSRLS, NOINHERIT
ExtensionExtension cardVersion, schema, Blocks icon
Policy (RLS)Policy cardCommand, roles, USING clause, WITH CHECK expression
Schema GroupColored containerGroups all objects belonging to a PostgreSQL schema namespace

Every object type can be shown or hidden independently — see Visibility Controls.

Table Nodes in Detail¶

Tables are the most information-dense nodes in the diagram. Each table card shows:

Column Rows¶

Every column row displays the column name, data type, and a set of constraint icons:

IconColorMeaning
🔑 KeyGold/yellowPrimary key column
🔗 LinkIndigoForeign key column (with edge drawn to referenced table)
✦ SparklesEmeraldUnique constraint
≡ ListAmberIndexed column
⚡ ZapIndigoGenerated column (GENERATED ALWAYS)

Column rows also show nullability (NOT NULL marked with red asterisk) and whether the type is an enum (ENUM badge).

Collapsible Sections¶

Expand any table node to reveal:

  • Indexes — index name, type (B-tree, GiST, GIN, etc.), uniqueness, and column coverage
  • Triggers — trigger name, timing (BEFORE/AFTER), events (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE), and function name
  • Policies — RLS policy name, command, applicable roles, USING and WITH CHECK expressions
  • Check Constraints — constraint name and the CHECK expression

View Modes¶

You can switch between three column display modes from the footer:

ModeWhat's shown
ALLEvery column with full metadata, all collapsible sections
KEYSOnly primary key and foreign key columns — compact overview
TITLETable name only — maximum density for very large schemas

Cascade Risk Indicator¶

If a table has a chain of ON DELETE CASCADE foreign keys that could affect many rows, the table node shows an amber/red glow border with a ⚡ badge and the count of tables in the cascade chain.

Editing Tables from the Diagram¶

You can edit any table's structure directly from the ER Diagram without switching to the SQL editor. Click the edit icon (pencil) on any table node header to open the Table Edit Panel. It supports two modes, switchable with a toggle:

Visual Editor¶

The visual mode lets you add, remove, or modify columns using a form interface — no SQL required. Each column row has fields for name, type, nullability, default value, and constraint toggles (PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY).

ControlWhat it does
Add columnAppends a new empty column row to the form
Delete columnRemoves the column (shows a confirmation for columns with FK dependencies)
Type selectorDropdown of all PostgreSQL types including your project's custom enums and domains
Constraint togglesToggle PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE per column
FK targetDrop-down of all tables and columns in the project

When you click Save, the edited table definition is serialized back to SQL and written into the active file. The ER Diagram re-renders immediately from the updated SQL.

SQL Editor Mode¶

Switch to the SQL tab in the edit panel to view and edit the raw CREATE TABLE DDL directly. This mode gives you full control — useful for complex constraints, partial indexes on the table, or multi-column primary keys.

Changes you make in SQL mode are validated before saving. If the SQL is invalid, the panel shows the parse error and prevents saving until it is fixed.

Bidirectional sync: Visual mode and SQL mode show the same table. Switching between modes converts the representation in real time — edits made in visual mode are immediately visible in SQL mode and vice versa.

Relationship Edges¶

Each foreign key is drawn as a directed edge from the referencing column to the referenced table:

Edge styleMeaning
Solid arrowStandard foreign key
Dashed arrowNullable FK (optional relationship)
Orange edgeView dependency (view references another object)
Red edgeTrigger target relationship
Low opacityLow-confidence inferred relationship (confidence < 0.8)

Click any edge to see a side panel with the FK column names, ON DELETE rule (CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT, NO ACTION), and deferrability.

Navigation¶

ActionHow
PanClick and drag the canvas background
Zoom in / outScroll wheel, or use + / − buttons in the toolbar
Fit all nodesClick Fit in the toolbar — centers and scales to show every node
Select a tableClick any node — highlights it and dims unrelated nodes
Move a nodeDrag a node to reposition — positions are saved per session
Reset layoutClick Layout → Re-run auto-layout to restore ELK positions
SearchType in the search box in the toolbar to filter visible nodes by name

Search¶

The toolbar search box filters the diagram in real time (300 ms debounce). Nodes whose names match the query stay visible; all others are dimmed. Matching is case-insensitive and partial.

Auto-Layout¶

The diagram uses ELK (Eclipse Layout Kernel) to position nodes automatically. ELK respects FK relationships and arranges parent tables above (or to the left of) their dependent tables.

Layout Direction¶

Switch layout direction from the toolbar dropdown:

DirectionDescription
Left → Right (LR)Parent tables on the left, child tables flow rightward — good for wide schemas
Top → Bottom (TB)Parent tables at the top, dependencies flow downward — good for deep hierarchies
Right → Left (RL)Mirrored LR
Bottom → Top (BT)Mirrored TB

Position Persistence¶

After ELK places nodes, you can drag any node to fine-tune its position. Positions are stored per schema (via Zustand) and restored when you return to the diagram. Click Reset layout to discard manual positions and re-run ELK from scratch.

Performance & Scale¶

The ELK engine has a built-in timeout system:

  • Hierarchical layout (with schema groups): 8-second timeout, then falls back to flat layout
  • Flat layout: 15-second timeout

For schemas with thousands of tables, use KEYS or TITLE view mode and Visibility Controls to hide object types you don't need — this significantly reduces node count and speeds up layout.

Toolbar Controls¶

ControlDescription
Search boxFilter visible nodes by name (real-time, debounced)
Layout ▾Switch layout direction (LR / TB / RL / BT)
Connect DBOpen the database connection panel
Export ▾Export diagram or schema (see below)
PathToggle path analysis mode — find shortest FK path between two tables
Resona AIOpen the global AI chat panel anchored to the diagram
FullscreenToggle fullscreen mode

Footer Controls¶

ControlDescription
Table / view / relationship countsLive stats of what's currently visible
Schema filter badgeShown in amber when any schemas are hidden — click to clear
View modeSwitch between ALL / KEYS / TITLE column display
Group ▾Toggle "Cluster by Schema" and "Lock Groups"
Visibility ▾Toggle individual node types and schema groups
TerminalOpen the SQL terminal panel (linked to a live database connection)

Export¶

Click Export in the toolbar to save the diagram or schema in multiple formats:

Image Exports¶

FormatDescription
PNGHigh-resolution raster image (2× pixel ratio) — good for Notion, docs, Slack
SVGScalable vector image — good for presentations and print

Schema Code Exports¶

The diagram can also generate framework-ready code from your schema:

FormatOutput fileUse case
Prisma Schemaschema.prismaDrop into a Prisma project
Drizzle ORMschema.tsDrop into a Drizzle project
DBMLschema.dbmlImport into dbdiagram.io
TypeScript Typestypes.tsType-safe interfaces matching your schema
Markdown DocsSCHEMA.mdHuman-readable schema documentation

All exports download as files with auto-generated names based on your project.

Focus Mode (Subgraph)¶

Click the Network icon on any table node to enter focus mode. The diagram zooms in on that table and its direct relationships, hiding the rest. You can control:

  • Depth — how many FK hops to follow from the root (1 = direct neighbors, 2 = two hops, up to 5)
  • Direction — outbound (tables this table references), inbound (tables that reference this table), or both
  • Confidence threshold — exclude low-confidence inferred relationships

A banner at the top of the diagram shows which table is focused. Click × to restore the full diagram.

Real-Time Updates¶

The diagram re-renders automatically every time the SQL parser produces a new result:

SQL changeDiagram change
CREATE TABLENew node appears
DROP TABLENode and all its edges disappear
Add REFERENCESNew directed edge appears
Rename a columnColumn row updates in place
Add an indexIndex row appears in the table's Indexes section
Add a policyPolicy row appears in the table's Policies section
Add an enumNew enum node appears with all values as badges

Next Steps¶

  • Path Analysis — find the shortest FK join path between any two tables
  • Grouping & Schema Clusters — cluster tables by PostgreSQL schema with resizable group containers
  • Resona AI in the ER Diagram — AI analysis anchored to individual tables, schema groups, or the whole schema
  • Visibility & Node Types — control which object types and schemas are shown
  • Schema Compiler — static analysis that grades your schema and surfaces issues
  • Schema Diff — compare two schema versions side-by-side

| ≡ List | Amber | Indexed column |
| ⚡ Zap | Indigo | Generated column (`GENERATED ALWAYS`) |

Column rows also show nullability (`NOT NULL` marked with red asterisk) and whether the type is an enum (ENUM badge).

### Collapsible Sections

Expand any table node to reveal:

- **Indexes** — index name, type (B-tree, GiST, GIN, etc.), uniqueness, and column coverage
- **Triggers** — trigger name, timing (BEFORE/AFTER), events (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE), and function name
- **Policies** — RLS policy name, command, applicable roles, USING and WITH CHECK expressions
- **Check Constraints** — constraint name and the CHECK expression

### View Modes

You can switch between three column display modes from the footer:

| Mode | What's shown |
|---|---|
| **ALL** | Every column with full metadata, all collapsible sections |
| **KEYS** | Only primary key and foreign key columns — compact overview |
| **TITLE** | Table name only — maximum density for very large schemas |

### Cascade Risk Indicator

If a table has a chain of `ON DELETE CASCADE` foreign keys that could affect many rows, the table node shows an amber/red glow border with a ⚡ badge and the count of tables in the cascade chain.

---

## Editing Tables from the Diagram

You can edit any table's structure directly from the ER Diagram without switching to the SQL editor. Click the **edit icon** (pencil) on any table node header to open the **Table Edit Panel**. It supports two modes, switchable with a toggle:

### Visual Editor

The visual mode lets you add, remove, or modify columns using a form interface — no SQL required. Each column row has fields for name, type, nullability, default value, and constraint toggles (PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY).

![The ER Diagram table editor in visual mode showing column fields, type selectors, and constraint toggles for a selected table](/images/sql-editor/er-diagram-edittable-visual.png)

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Add column** | Appends a new empty column row to the form |
| **Delete column** | Removes the column (shows a confirmation for columns with FK dependencies) |
| **Type selector** | Dropdown of all PostgreSQL types including your project's custom enums and domains |
| **Constraint toggles** | Toggle PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE per column |
| **FK target** | Drop-down of all tables and columns in the project |

When you click **Save**, the edited table definition is serialized back to SQL and written into the active file. The ER Diagram re-renders immediately from the updated SQL.

### SQL Editor Mode

Switch to the SQL tab in the edit panel to view and edit the raw `CREATE TABLE` DDL directly. This mode gives you full control — useful for complex constraints, partial indexes on the table, or multi-column primary keys.

![The ER Diagram table editor in SQL mode showing the raw CREATE TABLE DDL with syntax highlighting](/images/sql-editor/er-diagram-edit-sql.png)

Changes you make in SQL mode are validated before saving. If the SQL is invalid, the panel shows the parse error and prevents saving until it is fixed.

> **Bidirectional sync:** Visual mode and SQL mode show the same table. Switching between modes converts the representation in real time — edits made in visual mode are immediately visible in SQL mode and vice versa.

---

## Relationship Edges

Each foreign key is drawn as a directed edge from the referencing column to the referenced table:

| Edge style | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Solid arrow** | Standard foreign key |
| **Dashed arrow** | Nullable FK (optional relationship) |
| **Orange edge** | View dependency (view references another object) |
| **Red edge** | Trigger target relationship |
| **Low opacity** | Low-confidence inferred relationship (confidence < 0.8) |

Click any edge to see a side panel with the FK column names, `ON DELETE` rule (CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT, NO ACTION), and deferrability.

---

## Navigation

| Action | How |
|---|---|
| **Pan** | Click and drag the canvas background |
| **Zoom in / out** | Scroll wheel, or use `+` / `−` buttons in the toolbar |
| **Fit all nodes** | Click **Fit** in the toolbar — centers and scales to show every node |
| **Select a table** | Click any node — highlights it and dims unrelated nodes |
| **Move a node** | Drag a node to reposition — positions are saved per session |
| **Reset layout** | Click **Layout → Re-run auto-layout** to restore ELK positions |
| **Search** | Type in the search box in the toolbar to filter visible nodes by name |

### Search

The toolbar search box filters the diagram in real time (300 ms debounce). Nodes whose names match the query stay visible; all others are dimmed. Matching is case-insensitive and partial.

---

## Auto-Layout

The diagram uses **ELK** (Eclipse Layout Kernel) to position nodes automatically. ELK respects FK relationships and arranges parent tables above (or to the left of) their dependent tables.

### Layout Direction

Switch layout direction from the toolbar dropdown:

| Direction | Description |
|---|---|
| **Left → Right (LR)** | Parent tables on the left, child tables flow rightward — good for wide schemas |
| **Top → Bottom (TB)** | Parent tables at the top, dependencies flow downward — good for deep hierarchies |
| **Right → Left (RL)** | Mirrored LR |
| **Bottom → Top (BT)** | Mirrored TB |

### Position Persistence

After ELK places nodes, you can drag any node to fine-tune its position. Positions are stored per schema (via Zustand) and restored when you return to the diagram. Click **Reset layout** to discard manual positions and re-run ELK from scratch.

### Performance & Scale

The ELK engine has a built-in timeout system:
- **Hierarchical layout** (with schema groups): 8-second timeout, then falls back to flat layout
- **Flat layout**: 15-second timeout

For schemas with thousands of tables, use **KEYS** or **TITLE** view mode and **Visibility Controls** to hide object types you don't need — this significantly reduces node count and speeds up layout.

---

## Toolbar Controls

| Control | Description |
|---|---|
| **Search box** | Filter visible nodes by name (real-time, debounced) |
| **Layout ▾** | Switch layout direction (LR / TB / RL / BT) |
| **Connect DB** | Open the database connection panel |
| **Export ▾** | Export diagram or schema (see below) |
| **Path** | Toggle path analysis mode — find shortest FK path between two tables |
| **Resona AI** | Open the global AI chat panel anchored to the diagram |
| **Fullscreen** | Toggle fullscreen mode |

---

## Footer Controls

| Control | Description |
|---|---|
| **Table / view / relationship counts** | Live stats of what's currently visible |
| **Schema filter badge** | Shown in amber when any schemas are hidden — click to clear |
| **View mode** | Switch between ALL / KEYS / TITLE column display |
| **Group ▾** | Toggle "Cluster by Schema" and "Lock Groups" |
| **Visibility ▾** | Toggle individual node types and schema groups |
| **Terminal** | Open the SQL terminal panel (linked to a live database connection) |

---

## Export

Click **Export** in the toolbar to save the diagram or schema in multiple formats:

### Image Exports

| Format | Description |
|---|---|
| **PNG** | High-resolution raster image (2× pixel ratio) — good for Notion, docs, Slack |
| **SVG** | Scalable vector image — good for presentations and print |

### Schema Code Exports

The diagram can also generate framework-ready code from your schema:

| Format | Output file | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| **Prisma Schema** | `schema.prisma` | Drop into a Prisma project |
| **Drizzle ORM** | `schema.ts` | Drop into a Drizzle project |
| **DBML** | `schema.dbml` | Import into dbdiagram.io |
| **TypeScript Types** | `types.ts` | Type-safe interfaces matching your schema |
| **Markdown Docs** | `SCHEMA.md` | Human-readable schema documentation |

All exports download as files with auto-generated names based on your project.

---

## Focus Mode (Subgraph)

Click the **Network icon** on any table node to enter focus mode. The diagram zooms in on that table and its direct relationships, hiding the rest. You can control:

- **Depth** — how many FK hops to follow from the root (1 = direct neighbors, 2 = two hops, up to 5)
- **Direction** — outbound (tables this table references), inbound (tables that reference this table), or both
- **Confidence threshold** — exclude low-confidence inferred relationships

A banner at the top of the diagram shows which table is focused. Click × to restore the full diagram.

---

## Real-Time Updates

The diagram re-renders automatically every time the SQL parser produces a new result:

| SQL change | Diagram change |
|---|---|
| `CREATE TABLE` | New node appears |
| `DROP TABLE` | Node and all its edges disappear |
| Add `REFERENCES` | New directed edge appears |
| Rename a column | Column row updates in place |
| Add an index | Index row appears in the table's Indexes section |
| Add a policy | Policy row appears in the table's Policies section |
| Add an enum | New enum node appears with all values as badges |

---

## Next Steps

- [Path Analysis](/sql-editor/er-diagram-path-analysis) — find the shortest FK join path between any two tables
- [Grouping & Schema Clusters](/sql-editor/er-diagram-grouping) — cluster tables by PostgreSQL schema with resizable group containers
- [Resona AI in the ER Diagram](/sql-editor/er-diagram-ai) — AI analysis anchored to individual tables, schema groups, or the whole schema
- [Visibility & Node Types](/sql-editor/er-diagram-visibility) — control which object types and schemas are shown
- [Schema Compiler](/sql-editor/schema-compiler) — static analysis that grades your schema and surfaces issues
- [Schema Diff](/sql-editor/schema-diff) — compare two schema versions side-by-side

sql-editor/file-manager.content:
File Manager¶

The SQL Editor's file manager lets you organize your PostgreSQL schema definitions into projects, folders, and files. It works like a lightweight version of VS Code's Explorer sidebar — with drag-and-drop reordering, instant file search, and full cloud sync for team projects.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · SQL Editor Overview · Collaboration

Dashboard — Your Project Workspace¶

When you first open the SQL Editor, you land on the Dashboard. This is the home screen for all your projects.

The Dashboard and the full file manager are both available in fullscreen mode — click the expand icon in the editor header to fill your entire browser window with the workspace.

Project List¶

Every project appears as a card showing its name, storage type, and team status. Click a project to see its details on the right panel. The currently opened project is marked with a green OPENED badge.

BadgeMeaning
CLOUDProject stored in Schema Weaver's backend — synced across devices
LOCALProject stored in your browser only — single device, no sharing
TEAMProject belongs to a team workspace
OPENEDThis project is the active project in the editor

Project Detail Panel¶

Selecting a project on the left reveals its details:

FieldDescription
FILESTotal number of SQL files in the project
FOLDERSNumber of folders (excluding the root)
MEMBERSNumber of team members with access
DATABASEName of the linked PostgreSQL connection, if any
STRUCTUREAuto-generated tree preview of folders and files

Click Open in Editor → to load the project into the editor and begin working.

Creating a Project¶

Click New in the dashboard header to open the project creation dialog.

FieldRequiredDescription
NameYesDisplay name for the project (e.g. payments-service)
DescriptionNoShort summary shown in the dashboard
TeamNoAssign to a team workspace for shared access
DatabaseNoLink a PostgreSQL connection at creation time

After creating the project you land directly in the editor with an empty project ready for files.

Explorer Sidebar¶

Once a project is open, the left sidebar switches from the dashboard to the Explorer view. This is your file tree for the active project. The sidebar is fully visible in fullscreen mode, giving you the complete project file tree alongside the editor and diagram without any distractions.

Sections¶

SectionDescription
Back arrowReturns to the dashboard, closing the active project
Filter filesSearch box — type to instantly filter file and folder names
OPEN EDITORSFiles currently open in tabs, in order of last access
PROJECT FILESFull file tree of the active project

File Tree Actions¶

Hover over any file or folder to reveal context actions:

ActionHow to trigger
New fileClick + in the PROJECT FILES header, or right-click a folder
New folderClick the folder-plus icon in the PROJECT FILES header
RenameRight-click a file/folder → Rename, or press F2 after selecting
DeleteRight-click → Delete (shows a confirmation dialog)
MoveDrag a file or folder to a new parent location
Collapse allClick the collapse icon in the section header

Creating Files and Folders¶

New File Dialog¶

When you create a new file you'll be prompted for:

FieldDescription
NameThe file name (e.g. users) — the .sql extension is added automatically
ExtensionFile type: sql (default), pgsql, or txt
LocationThe folder this file belongs to (defaults to the project root)

The file opens immediately in a tab after creation and is auto-named inline so you can start typing right away.

New Folder Dialog¶

Folder names follow the same pattern — enter a name, pick the parent location, and the folder appears expanded in the tree.

Folder Templates¶

For common patterns, use New Folder from Template to create a pre-structured folder hierarchy in one step:

TemplateCreates
Migration projectmigrations/, seeds/, schema/
Service schematables/, views/, functions/, triggers/
CustomEnter your own subfolder names

Fullscreen Split View¶

In fullscreen mode you can open a split panel to view two panes side by side — for example, your SQL file on the left and the live ER diagram on the right. This is the recommended way to work on large or complex schemas.

Click the split icon in the editor toolbar to activate split view:

Once open, the split panel shows the ER diagram updating in real time as you type — every table and relationship renders instantly without leaving the editor:

Drag and Drop¶

Files and folders can be dragged to reorganize the project:

  • Drag a file into any folder to move it there
  • Drag a file to the root area (below all folders) to move it to the top level
  • Drag a folder to nest it inside another folder
  • The tree updates immediately with an optimistic move; the server is updated in the background

File Search¶

The Filter files search box at the top of the Explorer filters the tree as you type. Matching files and their parent folders remain visible; non-matching items are hidden.

  • Searches file and folder names (case-insensitive)
  • Matching parent folders expand automatically to show matched children
  • Press Escape to clear the search and restore the full tree

Cloud vs Local Projects¶

Cloud Projects¶

Cloud projects are stored in Schema Weaver's backend (Supabase) and have these properties:

  • Synced across all your devices
  • Shareable with team members
  • Support version history and snapshots
  • Show a CLOUD badge in the dashboard
  • Require a Schema Weaver account

Local Projects¶

Local projects live entirely in your browser's storage:

  • No account required
  • Not synced between devices
  • Limited to 10 files (guest/local limit)
  • Show a LOCAL badge in the dashboard
  • Can be migrated to a cloud project at any time

Migrating Local to Cloud¶

When you sign in with an existing local project, Schema Weaver offers to migrate it:

  1. Click Migrate to Cloud when prompted
  2. Review the files that will be uploaded
  3. Confirm — files are uploaded and a new cloud project is created
  4. The local copy is cleaned up automatically

Recent Files¶

The dashboard shows your 8 most recently accessed files across all projects. Click any recent file to jump directly to it, reopening the parent project if needed.

Bulk Operations¶

Select multiple files by enabling Selection Mode (checkbox icon in the PROJECT FILES header):

OperationDescription
Bulk deleteDelete all selected files at once (confirmation required)
Bulk moveDrag all selected files to a new folder simultaneously
Click + ShiftSelect a range of consecutive files

Next Steps¶

  • Writing SQL — editor tabs, syntax highlighting, autosave, split view
  • Collaboration — invite team members, manage roles, share projects
  • Connector — link a project to a live PostgreSQL database
  • Version History — browse and restore past snapshots of any file

headings.title: What can you do in the SQL Editor?

sql-editor.content:
SQL Editor¶

The SQL Editor is the primary workspace in Schema Weaver. It's where you write PostgreSQL schema definitions, organize them into projects and files, analyze your schema quality with the built-in compiler, and visualize table relationships as an interactive ER diagram — all in one place.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · Docs Home · Data Explorer · Schema Weaver Landing

What can you do in the SQL Editor?¶

CapabilityDescription
Multi-file projectsOrganize schemas into cloud projects with folders and files
Syntax-highlighted editingPostgreSQL-aware editor with color coding and auto-indent
Tab-based workflowOpen multiple files simultaneously, switch between them instantly
Schema Compiler20-layer static analysis that grades your schema A–F and surfaces issues
ER DiagramAuto-generated visual diagram of tables and relationships from your SQL
Schema DiffSide-by-side comparison of two schema states with visual highlighting
Version HistoryBrowse and restore every saved snapshot of your files
Resona AIGenerate SQL with natural language, explain schemas, and review diffs
Database ConnectionsLink your project to a live PostgreSQL database for drift detection and migrations — managed in the Connector section
Team CollaborationInvite members to a project with read, write, or admin roles

Interface Layout¶

Left Sidebar — Explorer¶

RegionPurpose
Project nameShows the active project with a back arrow to return to the dashboard
PROJECT FILESCollapsible tree of all files and folders in the active project
OPEN EDITORSQuick list of currently open tabs
Filter filesInstant search across all file and folder names
Action iconsNew file, new folder, collapse all, toggle sidebar

Center — Editor¶

The main code editing area with syntax highlighting, tab management, and split/fullscreen controls. Each open file gets its own tab in the header bar.

Bottom — Status Bar¶

ButtonOpens
ConnectDatabase connection panel — link to a live PostgreSQL database
CompilerSchema analysis panel with grade, issue list, and recommendations
DiffSide-by-side schema diff between two SQL states
GraphER diagram visualizing all tables and relationships

Core Concepts¶

Projects¶

A project is the top-level container for related schema files. Projects can be:

  • Cloud — Stored in Schema Weaver's backend, accessible from any device, shareable with teams
  • Local — Stored in your browser, single-device only, no sharing

Each project has its own folder structure, file set, and optional database connection.

Files and Folders¶

Inside a project you can create any hierarchy of folders and .sql files. The SQL Editor merges all files in a project when computing the ER diagram, running the Schema Compiler, and preparing migration diffs — so you can split your schema across as many files as makes sense for your team.

The Compilation Pipeline¶

Every time you type SQL, the editor:

  1. Parses the SQL using a multi-phase PostgreSQL parser
  2. Merges all project files into a single schema
  3. Compiles the merged schema through 20 analysis layers
  4. Renders the ER diagram from the compiled output
  5. Grades the schema and surfaces any detected issues

This all happens in the browser — no server round-trips required for the analysis.

Supported PostgreSQL Objects¶

Object TypeSupport
Tables✅ Full — columns, constraints, defaults
Indexes✅ Full — B-tree, GiST, GIN, partial, expression
Views✅ Full — regular and materialized
Functions & Procedures✅ Full — PL/pgSQL, SQL, argument types
Triggers✅ Full — row/statement, BEFORE/AFTER/INSTEAD OF
Row-Level Security✅ Full — policies, enforcement
Enums & Custom Types✅ Full — enums, domains, composite, range
Foreign Keys✅ Full — with cascade rules and relationship visualization
Sequences✅ Full — identity columns, serial detection
Extensions✅ Detected — pgcrypto, uuid-ossp, PostGIS, etc.
Partitions✅ Full — RANGE, LIST, HASH, inheritance trees
Schemas (namespaces)✅ Supported — multi-schema projects

Quick Start¶

  1. Open sql-editor.schemaweaver.dev and sign in
  2. Click New on the dashboard to create your first project
  3. Create a file (e.g. schema.sql) inside the project
  4. Paste or write your PostgreSQL CREATE TABLE statements
  5. Watch the ER diagram build automatically in the Graph panel
  6. Open Compiler in the footer to see your schema grade and any detected issues
  7. Optionally link a live database with Connect to enable drift detection

Next Steps¶

  • File Manager — projects, cloud storage, folders, drag-and-drop
  • Writing SQL — tabs, syntax highlighting, autosave, split view
  • Schema Compiler — grades, issues, 20-layer analysis
  • ER Diagram — visual schema, layout, subgraphs, path analysis
  • Schema Diff — comparing schema versions side-by-side
  • Version History — browsing and restoring past snapshots
  • Resona AI — SQL generation, explanations, and review
  • Connector — connect to a live PostgreSQL database, run migrations, and detect drift
  • Collaboration — team projects, member roles, sharing

Analyze Live Data¶

Once your schema is designed, use the SW Data Explorer to browse live rows, run natural-language queries with Resona AI, and build a dashboard of metrics from your data.

# SQL Editor

The SQL Editor is the primary workspace in Schema Weaver. It's where you write PostgreSQL schema definitions, organize them into projects and files, analyze your schema quality with the built-in compiler, and visualize table relationships as an interactive ER diagram — all in one place.

> Quick links: [Open SQL Editor](https://sql-editor.schemaweaver.dev/) · [Docs Home](https://docs.schemaweaver.dev/) · [Data Explorer](https://docs.schemaweaver.dev/data-explorer/) · [Schema Weaver Landing](https://schemaweaver.dev/)

![The Schema Weaver SQL Editor showing the Explorer sidebar, multi-file tabs, SQL code editor, and the ER diagram panel](/images/sql-editor/sql-editor.png)

---

## What can you do in the SQL Editor?

| Capability | Description |
|---|---|
| **Multi-file projects** | Organize schemas into cloud projects with folders and files |
| **Syntax-highlighted editing** | PostgreSQL-aware editor with color coding and auto-indent |
| **Tab-based workflow** | Open multiple files simultaneously, switch between them instantly |
| **Schema Compiler** | 20-layer static analysis that grades your schema A–F and surfaces issues |
| **ER Diagram** | Auto-generated visual diagram of tables and relationships from your SQL |
| **Schema Diff** | Side-by-side comparison of two schema states with visual highlighting |
| **Version History** | Browse and restore every saved snapshot of your files |
| **Resona AI** | Generate SQL with natural language, explain schemas, and review diffs |
| **Database Connections** | Link your project to a live PostgreSQL database for drift detection and migrations — managed in the [Connector](/connector) section |
| **Team Collaboration** | Invite members to a project with read, write, or admin roles |

---

## Interface Layout

![The Schema Weaver SQL Editor showing the Explorer sidebar, multi-file tabs, SQL code editor, and the ER diagram panel](/images/sql-editor/sql-editor.png)

### Left Sidebar — Explorer

| Region | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Project name** | Shows the active project with a back arrow to return to the dashboard |
| **PROJECT FILES** | Collapsible tree of all files and folders in the active project |
| **OPEN EDITORS** | Quick list of currently open tabs |
| **Filter files** | Instant search across all file and folder names |
| **Action icons** | New file, new folder, collapse all, toggle sidebar |

### Center — Editor

The main code editing area with syntax highlighting, tab management, and split/fullscreen controls. Each open file gets its own tab in the header bar.

### Bottom — Status Bar

| Button | Opens |
|---|---|
| **Connect** | Database connection panel — link to a live PostgreSQL database |
| **Compiler** | Schema analysis panel with grade, issue list, and recommendations |
| **Diff** | Side-by-side schema diff between two SQL states |
| **Graph** | ER diagram visualizing all tables and relationships |

---

## Core Concepts

### Projects

A **project** is the top-level container for related schema files. Projects can be:

- **Cloud** — Stored in Schema Weaver's backend, accessible from any device, shareable with teams
- **Local** — Stored in your browser, single-device only, no sharing

Each project has its own folder structure, file set, and optional database connection.

### Files and Folders

Inside a project you can create any hierarchy of folders and `.sql` files. The SQL Editor **merges all files in a project** when computing the ER diagram, running the Schema Compiler, and preparing migration diffs — so you can split your schema across as many files as makes sense for your team.

### The Compilation Pipeline

Every time you type SQL, the editor:

1. **Parses** the SQL using a multi-phase PostgreSQL parser
2. **Merges** all project files into a single schema
3. **Compiles** the merged schema through 20 analysis layers
4. **Renders** the ER diagram from the compiled output
5. **Grades** the schema and surfaces any detected issues

This all happens in the browser — no server round-trips required for the analysis.

---

## Supported PostgreSQL Objects

| Object Type | Support |
|---|---|
| Tables | ✅ Full — columns, constraints, defaults |
| Indexes | ✅ Full — B-tree, GiST, GIN, partial, expression |
| Views | ✅ Full — regular and materialized |
| Functions & Procedures | ✅ Full — PL/pgSQL, SQL, argument types |
| Triggers | ✅ Full — row/statement, BEFORE/AFTER/INSTEAD OF |
| Row-Level Security | ✅ Full — policies, enforcement |
| Enums & Custom Types | ✅ Full — enums, domains, composite, range |
| Foreign Keys | ✅ Full — with cascade rules and relationship visualization |
| Sequences | ✅ Full — identity columns, serial detection |
| Extensions | ✅ Detected — pgcrypto, uuid-ossp, PostGIS, etc. |
| Partitions | ✅ Full — RANGE, LIST, HASH, inheritance trees |
| Schemas (namespaces) | ✅ Supported — multi-schema projects |

---

## Quick Start

1. Open [sql-editor.schemaweaver.dev](https://sql-editor.schemaweaver.dev/) and sign in
2. Click **New** on the dashboard to create your first project
3. Create a file (e.g. `schema.sql`) inside the project
4. Paste or write your PostgreSQL `CREATE TABLE` statements
5. Watch the ER diagram build automatically in the **Graph** panel
6. Open **Compiler** in the footer to see your schema grade and any detected issues
7. Optionally link a live database with **Connect** to enable drift detection

---

## Next Steps

- [File Manager](/sql-editor/file-manager) — projects, cloud storage, folders, drag-and-drop
- [Writing SQL](/sql-editor/writing-sql) — tabs, syntax highlighting, autosave, split view
- [Schema Compiler](/sql-editor/schema-compiler) — grades, issues, 20-layer analysis
- [ER Diagram](/sql-editor/er-diagram) — visual schema, layout, subgraphs, path analysis
- [Schema Diff](/sql-editor/schema-diff) — comparing schema versions side-by-side
- [Version History](/sql-editor/version-history) — browsing and restoring past snapshots
- [Resona AI](/sql-editor/ai-assistant) — SQL generation, explanations, and review
- [Connector](/connector) — connect to a live PostgreSQL database, run migrations, and detect drift
- [Collaboration](/team-collaboration) — team projects, member roles, sharing

---

### Analyze Live Data
Once your schema is designed, use the [SW Data Explorer](/data-explorer) to browse live rows, run natural-language queries with Resona AI, and build a dashboard of metrics from your data.

sql-editor/schema-compiler.content:
Schema Compiler¶

The Schema Compiler is a static analysis engine built into the SQL Editor. Every time you edit a file, it silently re-compiles the merged project SQL through 20 analysis layers and produces a health grade with a detailed issue report — all in your browser, with no server round-trip.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · SQL Editor Overview · Writing SQL

Opening the Compiler Panel¶

Click Compiler in the footer status bar to open the analysis panel. The button also shows a color-coded grade badge so you can see your schema health at a glance without opening the panel.

BadgeGradeMeaning
🟢 A90–100Excellent — production-ready
🟢 B80–89Good — minor issues
🟡 C70–79Acceptable — some gaps to address
🟠 D60–69Needs work — multiple issues present
🔴 F< 60Critical — blocking issues detected

What the Compiler Checks¶

The compiler processes your schema through 20 layers in sequence. Each layer analyzes a specific aspect of your PostgreSQL objects.

Layer Overview¶

#LayerWhat it analyzes
1DatabaseEncoding, server version, installed extensions
2SchemasNamespace-level object counts and anomalies
3TablesTable definitions, missing PKs, naming conventions
4ColumnsTypes, nullability, default values, text vs bounded types
5TypesEnums, domains, composite types, range types
6ConstraintsPKs, FKs, unique, check, exclusion constraints
7IndexesRedundant indexes, missing indexes on FK columns, expression indexes
8PartitionsPartition hierarchies, orphaned child tables
9ViewsBroken references, circular dependencies, materialized view freshness
10FunctionsSecurity definers, mutable functions in indexes, volatile defaults
11TriggersEvent trigger ordering conflicts, duplicate triggers
12RLSRow-level security coverage, policies without USING clauses
13PrivilegesOver-privileged roles, public schema exposure scoring
14SequencesOrphan sequences, mismatched identity columns
15ExtensionsInstalled vs available extensions, version mismatches
16DependenciesObject dependency graph, circular references
17StorageTable bloat estimates, TOAST configuration
18ReplicationReplication slot status, tables without REPLICA IDENTITY
19SemanticNaming convention consistency, plural/singular table names
20MetricsFinal health score, complexity rating, overall grade

Issue Severity Levels¶

Every detected issue is tagged with a severity:

SeverityColorWhen to act
Critical🔴 RedAct immediately — blocks production use
Warning🟠 OrangeAddress before the next release
Info🔵 BlueBest-practice suggestion — low urgency
Hint⚪ GrayOptional improvement — can safely ignore

Common Issues Detected¶

Tables & Columns¶

IssueSeverityDescription
Missing primary keyWarningTable has no PRIMARY KEY — replication and ORMs need one
Unbounded text columnInfoUse varchar(n) or a domain to document intent
Nullable foreign key without indexWarningCan cause sequential scans on joins
Column with no default or constraintHintExplicit NOT NULL or a DEFAULT documents intent clearly
serial instead of identityHintGENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is the modern alternative to serial

Indexes¶

IssueSeverityDescription
Redundant indexWarningAn index is a prefix of another — one can be dropped
Missing FK indexWarningForeign key column has no index — join performance will suffer
Unused expression indexInfoExpression indexes should be validated against real query plans
Duplicate indexCriticalTwo identical indexes waste storage and slow writes

Foreign Keys & Constraints¶

IssueSeverityDescription
FK references non-PK columnWarningFK target should be a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE column
Check constraint always trueInfoTautological CHECK clauses add noise with no benefit
Missing ON DELETE ruleHintExplicit cascade behavior is safer than implicit NO ACTION

Security¶

IssueSeverityDescription
RLS enabled but no policiesCriticalAll rows are blocked — queries will return empty results
SECURITY DEFINER functionWarningRuns with owner privileges — review for privilege escalation risk
PUBLIC schema accessibleWarningAll authenticated users can create objects in public — restrict with REVOKE
Table without RLS in a multi-tenant schemaInfoConsider enabling RLS for tenant isolation

Views & Functions¶

IssueSeverityDescription
View references dropped tableCriticalView will fail at query time
Circular view dependencyCriticalTwo views reference each other — this cannot be resolved at runtime
VOLATILE function in indexCriticalNon-deterministic functions cannot be used in expression indexes
Materialized view with no unique indexWarningREFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY requires a unique index

Reading the Compiler Panel¶

The panel is split into three sections:

1. Summary Bar¶

Schema Health      Grade: B      Score: 83 / 100
────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔴 Critical   0    🟠 Warning   3    🔵 Info   7    ⚪ Hint  12

2. Issue List¶

Issues are grouped by severity. Each entry shows:

ElementDescription
Icon + severityColor-coded severity indicator
Object nameThe table, column, index, or function the issue relates to
MessageA plain-English description of the problem
CategoryWhich layer detected this issue (e.g. indexes, rls, constraints)
Fix suggestionAn example SQL statement that would resolve the issue

Click any issue to jump directly to the relevant object in the SQL editor.

3. Metrics Summary¶

  Tables         24     Columns       187     Indexes        31
  Views           3     Functions       8     Triggers        5
  Enums           4     Policies        6     Extensions      3
  Complexity    HIGH     Replication  PARTIAL  Overall   GOOD

How the Grade is Calculated¶

The grade is computed from a weighted score across all 20 layers:

Score = Σ (layer_weight × layer_score) / Σ layer_weights

Layer weights (highest → lowest):
  Constraints (20%) → Tables (15%) → Security/RLS (15%) →
  Indexes (12%) → Functions (10%) → Views (8%) →
  Columns (8%) → Remaining layers (12% combined)

Each critical issue reduces the score by 5–15 points. Warnings reduce by 1–3 points. Info and hints do not affect the numeric score.

Compiler in the Workflow¶

The compiler runs automatically every time you stop typing (debounced at 500 ms). You don't need to trigger it manually.

You type SQL  →  Parser runs  →  Compiler runs  →  Grade updates in footer

The ER diagram also re-renders from the same compilation output, so diagram and analysis are always in sync with your code.

Example: Fixing a Warning¶

Given this schema:

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id   serial,
  user uuid REFERENCES users(id)
);

The compiler would flag:

  • orders — Warning: Missing primary key
  • orders.id — Hint: Use GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY instead of serial
  • orders.user — Warning: FK column user has no index

Fixed version:

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id      integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id uuid    NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders (user_id);

After applying the fix, the grade improves and all three issues disappear.

Next Steps¶

  • ER Diagram — visualize the compiled schema as an interactive relationship diagram
  • Schema Diff — compare two versions of your schema
  • Connector — run migrations against a live database
  • Writing SQL — editor tabs, syntax highlighting, and autosave

Verify Data Health¶

Use the SW Data Explorer to ensure your schema supports real-world data queries and browse live rows from your newly audited tables.

sql-editor/schema-diff.content:
Schema Diff¶

The Schema Diff tool lets you compare two PostgreSQL schema states side-by-side. It highlights every added, removed, and modified object — tables, columns, indexes, constraints, and more — so you can review changes before applying a migration or audit what drifted in production.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · SQL Editor Overview · Version History

Opening the Diff Panel¶

Click Diff in the footer status bar to open the diff panel. You can also access it from the Schema Diff option in the top toolbar.

Choosing What to Diff¶

The diff panel has two selectors — Left (Base) and Right (Head) — which define what you are comparing.

SourceDescription
Current fileThe SQL currently in the editor for the selected file
Version snapshotA saved historical snapshot of a file (from version history)
Live databaseThe current schema pulled from a connected PostgreSQL database
ClipboardPaste any SQL directly into the diff input

Common diff scenarios:

ScenarioLeftRight
Review uncommitted editsSaved snapshotCurrent file
Preview a migrationCurrent projectLive database
Audit production driftLive databaseLast deployed snapshot
Review a teammate's PRMain branch snapshotPR branch snapshot

The Diff View¶

Once both sides are selected, the diff renders in three ways depending on your preference:

Unified Diff (default)¶

A single-column view with additions and removals interleaved:

  CREATE TABLE users (
    id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    email       text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
+   username    text,
-   full_name   text NOT NULL,
+   display_name text,
    created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
  );

+ CREATE INDEX idx_users_username ON users (username);
ColorMeaning
🟢 Green line (prefix +)Added — present in Right but not Left
🔴 Red line (prefix -)Removed — present in Left but not Right
⚪ White lineUnchanged context

Side-by-side Diff¶

A two-column view with Left on the left and Right on the right. Changed lines are highlighted in their respective columns. Useful when reviewing large blocks of SQL where you want to read both versions simultaneously.

Semantic Diff¶

Rather than raw line-by-line comparison, the semantic diff understands SQL structure and reports changes at the object level:

MODIFIED  TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN    username text
  DROP COLUMN   full_name
  ADD COLUMN    display_name text

ADDED  INDEX idx_users_username
  ON users (username)

Semantic diff is noise-free — reformatting, reindentation, and comment changes are ignored. Only structural DDL changes appear.

Diff Summary Bar¶

At the top of the diff panel:

Changes:  + 3 added   ~ 2 modified   - 1 removed
Objects:    tables: 0   columns: 4   indexes: 1   constraints: 0
CounterDescription
AddedObjects present in Right but not Left
ModifiedObjects present in both but changed
RemovedObjects present in Left but not Right

Navigating the Diff¶

ActionHow
Jump to next changeClick ↓ in the diff toolbar or press Alt+↓
Jump to previous changeClick ↑ or press Alt+↑
Filter by change typeUse the + / ~ / - toggle buttons to show only adds, modifications, or removals
Filter by object typeUse the Tables / Columns / Indexes / Constraints chips to focus
Expand contextClick … between hunks to show more surrounding lines

Inline Diff Overlay¶

When you have a database connection active, an inline diff overlay can be shown directly inside the SQL editor (not just in the diff panel). Changed lines are highlighted with a colored gutter marker:

Gutter colorMeaning
🟢 Green barLine added vs the live database version
🔴 Red barLine present in the database but removed in your editor
🟡 Yellow barLine modified relative to the database version

This overlay makes it easy to see exactly what your current edits would change in production without switching away from the editor.

Toggle the overlay with Diff → Show inline diff in the footer.

Exporting a Diff¶

Click Export in the diff panel header to download the diff:

FormatUse case
Unified patch (.diff)Standard diff format — can be attached to a PR or stored in git
Migration SQLThe additions and modifications expressed as executable DDL statements
Markdown reportHuman-readable summary with a change table — useful for PR descriptions

Diff and Migrations¶

The diff between your current schema file and the live database is the foundation for Schema Weaver's migration engine. When you click Apply Migration from the connections panel, Schema Weaver:

  1. Runs a semantic diff between your project SQL and the live database schema
  2. Generates a safe migration plan (handling type casts, FK order, enum additions)
  3. Shows you the migration SQL for review before applying

See Connector for details on connecting to a live database and running migrations.

Next Steps¶

  • Version History — browse past snapshots to use as diff sources
  • Connector — diff your SQL against a live database
  • Schema Compiler — analyze your schema for issues before diffing
  • ER Diagram — visualize the structural changes alongside the diff

| Source | Description |
|---|---|
| **Current file** | The SQL currently in the editor for the selected file |
| **Version snapshot** | A saved historical snapshot of a file (from version history) |
| **Live database** | The current schema pulled from a connected PostgreSQL database |
| **Clipboard** | Paste any SQL directly into the diff input |

Common diff scenarios:

| Scenario | Left | Right |
|---|---|---|
| Review uncommitted edits | Saved snapshot | Current file |
| Preview a migration | Current project | Live database |
| Audit production drift | Live database | Last deployed snapshot |
| Review a teammate's PR | Main branch snapshot | PR branch snapshot |

---

## The Diff View

Once both sides are selected, the diff renders in three ways depending on your preference:

### Unified Diff (default)

A single-column view with additions and removals interleaved:

```diff
  CREATE TABLE users (
    id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    email       text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
+   username    text,
-   full_name   text NOT NULL,
+   display_name text,
    created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
  );

+ CREATE INDEX idx_users_username ON users (username);
```

| Color | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 🟢 Green line (prefix `+`) | Added — present in Right but not Left |
| 🔴 Red line (prefix `-`) | Removed — present in Left but not Right |
| ⚪ White line | Unchanged context |

### Side-by-side Diff

A two-column view with Left on the left and Right on the right. Changed lines are highlighted in their respective columns. Useful when reviewing large blocks of SQL where you want to read both versions simultaneously.

### Semantic Diff

Rather than raw line-by-line comparison, the semantic diff understands SQL structure and reports changes at the **object level**:

```
MODIFIED  TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN    username text
  DROP COLUMN   full_name
  ADD COLUMN    display_name text

ADDED  INDEX idx_users_username
  ON users (username)
```

Semantic diff is noise-free — reformatting, reindentation, and comment changes are ignored. Only structural DDL changes appear.

---

## Diff Summary Bar

At the top of the diff panel:

```
Changes:  + 3 added   ~ 2 modified   - 1 removed
Objects:    tables: 0   columns: 4   indexes: 1   constraints: 0
```

| Counter | Description |
|---|---|
| **Added** | Objects present in Right but not Left |
| **Modified** | Objects present in both but changed |
| **Removed** | Objects present in Left but not Right |

---

## Navigating the Diff

| Action | How |
|---|---|
| Jump to next change | Click `↓` in the diff toolbar or press `Alt+↓` |
| Jump to previous change | Click `↑` or press `Alt+↑` |
| Filter by change type | Use the **+** / **~** / **-** toggle buttons to show only adds, modifications, or removals |
| Filter by object type | Use the **Tables / Columns / Indexes / Constraints** chips to focus |
| Expand context | Click `…` between hunks to show more surrounding lines |

---

## Inline Diff Overlay

When you have a database connection active, an **inline diff overlay** can be shown directly inside the SQL editor (not just in the diff panel). Changed lines are highlighted with a colored gutter marker:

| Gutter color | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 🟢 Green bar | Line added vs the live database version |
| 🔴 Red bar | Line present in the database but removed in your editor |
| 🟡 Yellow bar | Line modified relative to the database version |

This overlay makes it easy to see exactly what your current edits would change in production without switching away from the editor.

Toggle the overlay with **Diff → Show inline diff** in the footer.

---

## Exporting a Diff

Click **Export** in the diff panel header to download the diff:

| Format | Use case |
|---|---|
| **Unified patch (.diff)** | Standard diff format — can be attached to a PR or stored in git |
| **Migration SQL** | The additions and modifications expressed as executable DDL statements |
| **Markdown report** | Human-readable summary with a change table — useful for PR descriptions |

---

## Diff and Migrations

The diff between your current schema file and the live database is the foundation for Schema Weaver's migration engine. When you click **Apply Migration** from the connections panel, Schema Weaver:

1. Runs a semantic diff between your project SQL and the live database schema
2. Generates a safe migration plan (handling type casts, FK order, enum additions)
3. Shows you the migration SQL for review before applying

See [Connector](/connector) for details on connecting to a live database and running migrations.

---

## Next Steps

- [Version History](/sql-editor/version-history) — browse past snapshots to use as diff sources
- [Connector](/connector) — diff your SQL against a live database
- [Schema Compiler](/sql-editor/schema-compiler) — analyze your schema for issues before diffing
- [ER Diagram](/sql-editor/er-diagram) — visualize the structural changes alongside the diff

sql-editor/version-history.content:
Version History¶

The SQL Editor keeps a complete snapshot history of every file in your cloud projects. Every save creates an immutable version entry — you can browse the timeline, compare any two snapshots, or restore a previous state with a single click.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · SQL Editor Overview · Schema Diff

Opening Version History¶

There are two ways to open the version history panel:

  1. Right-click any file in the Explorer sidebar → Version History
  2. Header menu → History when a file is active in the editor

The panel slides in from the right, showing the full timeline for the selected file.

The Version Timeline¶

The history panel lists every saved version of the file, newest first:

Version History — auth.sql
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 ● Today, 14:32    "Added sessions table"          You
 ● Today, 11:07    "Auto-save"                     You
 ● Yesterday 18:44 "Moved RLS policies to auth"    teammate@company.com
 ● Yesterday 09:12 "Initial schema"                You
 ● Apr 12, 22:30   "Auto-save"                     You
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Each entry shows:

FieldDescription
TimestampWhen the version was saved (relative for recent, absolute for older)
LabelA short description — auto-generated from the save context or manually set
AuthorThe team member who saved this version
Indicator● for the current version, ○ for historical

Viewing a Past Version¶

Click any version in the timeline to load it into a read-only preview in the main editor. The file tab shows auth.sql (v2024-04-12) to make it clear you're viewing a historical state.

While previewing a past version you can:

  • Read the SQL — full syntax highlighting, no editing
  • Copy any text
  • Diff against current — click Compare with current to open the diff panel with this snapshot as the Left side
  • Restore — click Restore this version to make this snapshot the active content of the file

Restoring a Version¶

Click Restore this version to replace the current file content with the selected snapshot.

This creates a new version entry at the top of the timeline with the label Restored from [timestamp] — the restore is non-destructive. If you restore by mistake, you can immediately restore the previous version.

 ● Just now        "Restored from Apr 12, 22:30"   You   ← new entry
 ● Today, 14:32    "Added sessions table"           You
 ● Today, 11:07    "Auto-save"                      You
   ...
 ● Apr 12, 22:30   "Initial schema"                 You   ← source

Labeling a Version¶

By default, save events are labeled Auto-save. You can add a meaningful label:

  1. Right-click any version → Edit label
  2. Type a description (e.g. Before adding audit triggers)
  3. Press Enter to save

Labels are visible to all team members with access to the project and are useful for milestone tracking (v1.0 launch schema, post-incident RLS fix, etc.).

Comparing Two Historical Versions¶

To compare any two snapshots (not just against current):

  1. Hover a version → click Pin as Left
  2. Click a second version → it becomes the Right side
  3. Click Compare — the diff panel opens with both snapshots loaded

This lets you answer questions like "What changed between last Tuesday and the version we deployed Friday?"

Version Retention¶

Project typeRetention
Cloud project (free tier)30 days of history
Cloud project (pro tier)Unlimited history
Local projectNo version history (local storage only)

How Versions Are Created¶

A new version is created whenever:

TriggerLabel
Autosave fires (after 3 seconds of inactivity)Auto-save
Manual save (Ctrl+S / Cmd+S)Manual save
File restored from a previous snapshotRestored from [timestamp]
Migration applied (snapshot before and after)Pre-migration snapshot / Post-migration snapshot
AI change acceptedAI-generated: [description]

Version History and Migrations¶

Every time a migration is applied through Schema Weaver's migration engine, two version entries are created automatically:

  • Pre-migration — a snapshot of the file immediately before the migration was applied
  • Post-migration — a snapshot reflecting the new state, with the migration ID as the label

This gives you a reliable rollback point for every migration event. If a migration causes unexpected issues, restore to the pre-migration snapshot, fix your SQL, and re-apply.

Next Steps¶

  • Schema Diff — compare any two version snapshots in the diff panel
  • Connector — migrations create automatic version snapshots
  • Writing SQL — autosave behavior and manual save
  • Collaboration — version history is shared with all team members on a project

sql-editor/writing-sql.content:
Writing SQL¶

The SQL Editor gives you a PostgreSQL-aware code editor with multi-file tabs, syntax highlighting, autosave, and a fullscreen mode. This page covers everything about the editing experience itself.

Quick links: Open SQL Editor · SQL Editor Overview · Schema Compiler

The Editor¶

The center panel is a fully featured code editor optimized for PostgreSQL schema definitions. It handles large files gracefully and keeps the interface responsive even with hundreds of tables.

The left sidebar is your file manager — project name, folder tree, open editors list, and file search all live here. Use it to navigate between files, create new ones, and organize your schema across folders.

Syntax Highlighting¶

The editor colors your SQL to make it immediately readable:

ColorElement
KeywordCREATE, TABLE, PRIMARY KEY, REFERENCES, NOT NULL, etc.
Typetext, uuid, timestamptz, integer, jsonb, boolean, etc.
StringString literals and quoted identifiers
Comment-- single line and /* block */ comments
NumberNumeric literals and constants
Operator=, ::, ->, ->>, @>, etc.

Auto-Indentation¶

The editor automatically indents new lines inside CREATE TABLE, BEGIN ... END, and function bodies. Pressing Enter after an opening ( indents the next line by one level.

Line Numbers¶

Line numbers are displayed in the left gutter. Clicking a line number selects the entire line.

Tabs — Working with Multiple Files¶

Each file you open gets its own tab in the header bar at the top of the editor.

│  auth.sql  ×  │  billing.sql  ×  │  schema.sql  ●  │  +  │
ElementMeaning
File nameThe name of the open file
×Close this tab
● (dot)This tab has unsaved changes
Italic namePreview tab — not yet pinned (single-click opens in preview, double-click pins)
+Open a new file or create a file

Tab Behavior¶

ActionResult
Single-click a file in the ExplorerOpens in a preview tab (italic) — replaces any existing preview
Double-click a file in the ExplorerOpens in a permanent tab
Double-click a preview tabPins the tab permanently
Close all tabsReturns to the welcome/dashboard view
Middle-click a tabCloses the tab

Tab Context Menu¶

Right-click any tab to access:

OptionDescription
CloseClose this tab
Close OthersClose all tabs except the current one
Close AllClose every open tab
Reveal in ExplorerScrolls and highlights the file in the left sidebar tree

Autosave¶

The editor autosaves your changes automatically. The footer status bar shows:

StatusMeaning
Autosave ✓Autosave is on — changes are saved a few seconds after you stop typing
Saving...A save is in progress
Saved + timestampThe last successful save time
Unsaved changesAutosave is off and there are pending changes

Toggle Autosave¶

Click the autosave indicator in the footer to toggle it on or off. When autosave is off, use Ctrl+S / Cmd+S to save manually.

Tip: Autosave uses optimistic conflict detection. If the server copy was updated by a team member since your last load, a conflict toast appears and lets you choose to overwrite or reload.

Fullscreen Mode¶

Click the fullscreen icon (↗) in the top-right of the editor header to expand the editor to fill the entire browser window.

In fullscreen mode:

  • The left Explorer sidebar appears, giving you the full file tree
  • The bottom status bar remains accessible
  • The ER diagram, compiler, and diff panels open as overlays
  • Press Escape or click the collapse icon to exit fullscreen

Tip: Fullscreen mode is the recommended way to work on large schemas. The sidebar and status bar give you everything you need without context-switching to other pages.

Split View¶

Click the split view icon in the header to open a second panel alongside the editor. The right panel shows the live ER diagram — every table and relationship updates instantly as you type SQL, giving you a real-time visual of your schema without switching views.

Split view is also used for:

  • Comparing two files side by side
  • Keeping the Resona AI chat panel open while you edit
  • Viewing the diff panel while reviewing changes

Drag the divider between panels to adjust the relative widths.

Keyboard Shortcuts¶

ShortcutAction
Ctrl+S / Cmd+SSave current file
Ctrl+Z / Cmd+ZUndo
Ctrl+Shift+Z / Cmd+Shift+ZRedo
Ctrl+/ / Cmd+/Toggle line comment (--)
Ctrl+D / Cmd+DSelect next occurrence of current word
Ctrl+F / Cmd+FFind in current file
Ctrl+H / Cmd+HFind and replace
Alt+↑ / Alt+↓Move current line up or down
Ctrl+Shift+K / Cmd+Shift+KDelete current line
Ctrl+EnterInsert line below without breaking the current line
TabIndent selected lines
Shift+TabUnindent selected lines

The Merge Model¶

The SQL Editor maintains a merged view of all files in the active project. This merged SQL is what feeds the parser, schema compiler, and ER diagram.

auth.sql     + billing.sql   + schema.sql
     ↓               ↓               ↓
           Merged SQL (in memory)
                    ↓
     SQL Parser → Schema Compiler → ER Diagram

This means:

  • You can split your schema across as many files as you like — the analysis always sees the full picture
  • A REFERENCES in billing.sql pointing to a table defined in auth.sql will resolve correctly
  • The order files are merged follows the folder structure (folders first, then files, alphabetically within each group)
  • Circular or missing references are caught and reported in the Compiler

Format Button¶

The Format button in the footer toolbar reformats the SQL in the current file:

  • Normalizes indentation and spacing
  • Uppercases SQL keywords
  • Wraps long lines at 100 characters
  • Preserves comments

Formatting is non-destructive — it only affects whitespace and casing, never the schema logic.

Generate Button¶

The Generate button opens the Resona AI SQL generation dialog. See Resona AI for full details.

Downloading Files¶

Right-click any file in the Explorer → Download to save it as a .sql file to your local machine. The download contains the raw SQL content of that file only (not the merged project SQL).

To export the full merged schema, use the Copy button in the footer toolbar — this copies the entire merged SQL to your clipboard.

File Extensions¶

The editor supports three file extensions:

ExtensionUse
.sqlStandard SQL — the default for all schema files
.pgsqlPostgreSQL-specific — same parsing and highlighting as .sql
.txtPlain text — useful for notes, changelogs, or documentation inside a project

Next Steps¶

  • Schema Compiler — analyze your SQL for issues, grades, and best practices
  • ER Diagram — visualize tables and relationships from your SQL
  • Schema Diff — compare two versions of your schema side-by-side
  • Version History — browse and restore past snapshots of any file
  • Resona AI — generate SQL from natural language descriptions

Right-click any file in the Explorer → **Download** to save it as a `.sql` file to your local machine. The download contains the raw SQL content of that file only (not the merged project SQL).

To export the full merged schema, use the **Copy** button in the footer toolbar — this copies the entire merged SQL to your clipboard.

---

## File Extensions

The editor supports three file extensions:

| Extension | Use |
|---|---|
| `.sql` | Standard SQL — the default for all schema files |
| `.pgsql` | PostgreSQL-specific — same parsing and highlighting as `.sql` |
| `.txt` | Plain text — useful for notes, changelogs, or documentation inside a project |

---

## Next Steps

- [Schema Compiler](/sql-editor/schema-compiler) — analyze your SQL for issues, grades, and best practices
- [ER Diagram](/sql-editor/er-diagram) — visualize tables and relationships from your SQL
- [Schema Diff](/sql-editor/schema-diff) — compare two versions of your schema side-by-side
- [Version History](/sql-editor/version-history) — browse and restore past snapshots of any file
- [Resona AI](/sql-editor/ai-assistant) — generate SQL from natural language descriptions
